blocks.html: 1.1 What Is Science?
Look around you right now. Something is happening everywhere you turn.

A fan is spinning. Sunlight is falling through a window and landing in a bright patch on the floor. Somewhere nearby, water is boiling, or a bird is calling, or dust is drifting through a beam of light. None of this is unusual. All of it is worth a second look.

You have been noticing things like this your whole life — why the moon seems to follow the car, why ice feels wet, why your shadow stretches long in the evening. Those questions were not childish. They were the beginning of something.
Now you are ready to go further.
An ordinary event can become a scientific question when you look closely.

Science is not a pile of facts to memorise. Science is a way of working. It means observing carefully, asking sharp questions, testing what you think you know, and being willing to change your mind when the evidence says you should.
Science Is Not Kept in a Building
Science does not live in laboratories. Laboratories are useful, but science is wherever something is happening.

blocks.html: It is in the kitchen, where heat turns a soft batter into a firm, holey dosa. It is on the cricket field, where a ball bends in the air because of the way it was spun. It is in the soil under a mango tree, where organisms too small to see are breaking down fallen leaves. It is inside your own body, where your heart is beating right now without being told to.
An Unfinished Map
Here is something surprising: science is not finished.

blocks.html: Think of what we know as a map of a huge, mostly unexplored land. Some regions are surveyed in fine detail. Others are sketched roughly. Some are still blank. And every time explorers map a new region, its edges open onto territory nobody knew existed. The map does not shrink the unknown — it reveals more of it.

Sometimes the mapmakers get it wrong. For centuries people were certain the Sun travelled around the Earth, because that is exactly what it looks like. Careful observation showed otherwise, and the map had to be redrawn. That correction was not a failure of science. It was science working as it should.
The Most Important Tool
You will use many instruments in this book — thermometers, magnets, lenses, balances. But the tool that matters most is not one you can hold. It is curiosity.

blocks.html: Curiosity is what makes you look up at a night sky and wonder what the stars actually are, and how far away. It is what makes you notice that a flower on your balcony is shut at dawn and open by mid-morning, and then wonder how it knows.

Why might this happen? A flower has no eyes and no clock. What could it be responding to? You do not need the right answer yet — only a reasonable guess. A possible explanation is a hypothesis. A prediction states what you expect to observe if it is right. For example, if light triggers opening, what should happen when the plant is shaded?
One Idea in Many Places

Some of what you learn in this book will be useful the same week you learn it. You will understand why food spoils faster in May than in December, why a frayed electrical wire is dangerous, how boiling kills many disease-causing microbes in water, while leaving dissolved chemical contaminants behind.
But the real reward comes later, and it is stranger than that.

Leave a wet shirt on a line and by evening it is dry. Pour water into an earthen matka and the water inside stays cool even on a hot afternoon. Watch the sky before the monsoon and see clouds thickening where there was clear blue an hour ago.
Three ordinary things. They seem to have nothing to do with each other.
Two involve evaporation directly; cloud formation needs another change as well.

blocks.html: In all three, water is leaving a liquid surface and moving into the air as an invisible vapour. That is what dries the shirt. That is what cools the matka — water seeping through the clay escapes from its surface and carries warmth away with it. Evaporation supplies water vapour. Clouds become visible when vapour cools and condenses into droplets or forms ice crystals; vapour itself is invisible.
Can you explain why? If evaporation cools the matka, what does that suggest about why you feel cold when you step out of a swimming pool into the wind?
Evaporation connects the shirt and the pot. Cloud formation also requires condensation or ice formation. Name each change rather than treating every water process as the same event.
Clouds become visible when cooling water vapour condenses into tiny droplets or forms ice crystals. Evaporation supplies the vapour; condensation helps form clouds.
A shared explanation can connect observations; check where it works and where another process is needed.
1.2 What This Book Will Ask You
Begin with the Earth — as far as we know, the only place in the universe where anything is alive.

blocks.html: A seed pushes a pale shoot up through dark soil. A caterpillar seals itself away and comes out with wings. A calf that could barely stand in the morning is running across the field by the end of the month. Growing is so ordinary that we stop noticing it happening. But how does a plant build an entire body out of soil, water and air?

Living things need materials and energy to grow. Green plants make sugars using light, water and carbon dioxide; animals obtain food by eating. In a country this large, that alone is a huge subject — pongal in one state, litti in another, a fish curry along the coast, a plate of rajma somewhere north. What are these dishes actually made of? And how could you find out for yourself, instead of being told?

Then there is water. You have jumped into a puddle after rain. But where was that water an hour before it fell on you, and how did it get up there? Cool it and it turns to ice. Heat it and it leaves as steam. What is going on?
And how hot is hot? When someone in your house has a fever, nobody wants a guess. They want a number.

Now look at what things are made of — paper, the metal of a key, a plastic scale, a rubber eraser, the magnet holding a cupboard shut, the cloth of your shirt. Each one was chosen for a reason. Could a key be made of rubber? Why not?
And when the Earth runs out of questions, there is the sky above it.

These questions connect different parts of science. Following water leads from a puddle to the weather. Studying a plant leads to light, air and food. Comparing materials leads to the design of useful objects. Look for these connections as you read. Ask what changes something, and what evidence could help explain it.
Every one of these has an answer. Not all of them are in this book.
You already do science. You have simply never called it that.
Suppose the clock on your wall has stopped. Both hands are frozen at ten past four.
The first thing you do is ask a question, even if only in your head: why has it stopped?

blocks.html: Then, almost without noticing, you make a guess. The cell inside must be finished.
Making a guess is the easy part. What matters is what you do next. You take the clock down, open the back, and fit a new cell.
If the hands begin to move, a used-up cell is one explanation. Refitting the cell also changed its contact with the terminals, so that observation alone does not prove which change mattered.
But suppose they do not move.

Now stop and notice something. The clock is still stopped, so it feels as though nothing has been achieved. That is not true. A failed replacement narrows the possibilities only if the new cell works, faces the right way and makes contact. Check these before ruling out the cell as a cause.
So you make a second guess. Perhaps the cell is fine but is not pressing properly against the metal contacts. You push it in firmly and give it a moment. Still nothing.
A third guess, then: something inside is stuck. You look more closely and find the thin second hand has caught against the minute hand and cannot pass it.
Question. Guess. Test. Look honestly at what happened. Guess again if you must.
Nobody sat you down and taught you that sequence. Yet it is very close to what a scientist does when facing something no one has ever explained.
The Steps Behind It
What you did with the clock has a name. It is called the scientific method, and written out plainly it looks like this:
1. Observe something that puzzles you or catches your interest.
2. Ask a question about it.
3. Guess a possible answer.
4. Test the guess, through an experiment or through further careful observation.
5. Examine the result and decide whether it actually answers your question.

That list looks tidier than real life ever is. Very often you finish step five only to discover you are back at step three with a fresh guess. Sometimes the test throws up something you were not even looking for, and that becomes a better question than the one you started with.

This is one useful route through an investigation, not a compulsory order for every kind of science. What matters is that the guess comes before the test, and that you accept the result even when it is not the one you wanted.
An observation describes what you notice: the clock hands have not moved. An explanation suggests a reason: the cell may be used up. Keeping these separate helps you test your idea honestly.

For a fair comparison, change one thing while keeping other conditions similar. If you replace the cell and free the hands together, you will not know which change mattered. Repeating a check can help you spot a result that happened only by chance.
Write about a problem you worked out for yourself recently. It does not have to be a science problem. List the steps you took, in order. Was there a point where you had to change your first guess?
Everyone Does This
Scientists follow the scientific method for a living. But nobody owns it, and it is used every day by people who would never call themselves scientists.

blocks.html: A cook lifts the lid off the idli batter in the morning and finds it flat instead of risen. She asks why. Was the kitchen too cold overnight? Was the batter ground too thin? She will not solve it by worrying — she will change one thing tomorrow and watch what happens.

art.svg: <svg class="science-illustration" width="186" height="133" viewBox="690 0 758 724" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet" overflow="hidden" data-original-bounds="{"x": 673.6229334765518, "y": 383.0001310909811, "w": 398.9999829605473, "h": 132.99979956378957}"><defs><clipPath id="se-art-clip-11"><rect x="690" y="0" width="758" height="724"/></clipPath></defs><image clip-path="url(#se-art-clip-11)" href="../../figures/class-6/science/ch01-p007-everyday-science.png" x="0" y="0" width="2172" height="724"><title>Tailor checking a needle</title></image></svg>

blocks.html: A tailor's machine starts skipping stitches. He does not replace the whole machine. He checks the needle first, then the thread tension, then the bobbin — one at a time, because changing everything at once would tell him nothing.

art.svg: <svg class="science-illustration" width="186" height="133" viewBox="1448 0 724 724" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet" overflow="hidden" data-original-bounds="{"x": 537.4999904412826, "y": 528.9998299616982, "w": 398.9999829605473, "h": 132.99979956379138}"><defs><clipPath id="se-art-clip-12"><rect x="1448" y="0" width="724" height="724"/></clipPath></defs><image clip-path="url(#se-art-clip-12)" href="../../figures/class-6/science/ch01-p007-everyday-science.png" x="0" y="0" width="2172" height="724"><title>Electrician checking a disconnected fitting</title></image></svg>

blocks.html: An electrician is called about a tubelight that flickers for a long time before it steadies. Is it the tube, the starter, or the wiring? Each of those can be tested separately.

None of them are in a laboratory. All of them are doing exactly what step three and step four describe: guess, then test — and crucially, test one thing at a time, so that the result actually means something.

A useful record is specific. Describe which part of a puddle’s edge moved and when. A sketch can preserve details that memory loses. Keep what you observed separate from your explanation of why it happened.
Choose one thing near your home that changes over time — a plant on a windowsill, a puddle after rain, ants around a spill, the shadow of a pole.
Watch it for five minutes without doing anything to it.
Write down three things you actually saw. Not what you think should happen — what happened.
Write one question your observation raised.
1.4 Curiosity, Company and a Long Road
Everything in this chapter rests on one habit, and it is not a difficult one. Notice things.

Noticing sounds too simple to matter. It is not. Most people walk past a hundred small oddities a day without registering a single one. The person who stops and says hold on, that's strange has done the hardest part already. Everything else — the questions, the guesses, the tests — follows from that pause.

And you do not have to do any of it alone. Science has a reputation for lonely geniuses, and it is mostly wrong. Discoveries today come from teams, often spread across many countries, arguing with one another and checking each other's work. Being told you are wrong by someone who has looked carefully at your evidence is not an insult. It is one of the most useful things that can happen to you.
So when you are stuck, ask someone. Compare what you saw with what your friend saw. If you disagree about what happened, that disagreement is worth more than either of your answers.

One last thing, and it is important. You will not find the answers to all your questions this year. Some of what you wonder about in Grade 6 you will only understand in Grade 9, or later, or possibly never — because nobody has worked it out yet.
That is not a warning. It is the best part.

Describe an event separately from a friend, then compare your accounts. Did you notice the same details? Which statements describe what you saw, and which suggest a reason? Differences give you something to check together. Finding an answer may need longer observation, a better comparison, or a more precise question.
Write down one "Why?" question about something you have noticed but never had explained. How might you begin to find the answer? Who could you ask, and what could you test?
Science begins with noticing. It continues with asking. And it never quite ends.
Go outside your classroom. Stand still for two minutes.
Look for grass in a crack, insects near a wall, or birds overhead. Choose two plants. Compare their leaves. What differences can you describe?
A planted tree and a plant growing without anyone sowing it both belong in your record. You do not need to know how something arrived before you can observe it.
This chapter is about that variety. How much of it is there? How do we make sense of it? And why are the living things in one place so different from the living things in another?
2.1 The Variety Around Us
A quick glance may tell you that a tree is there. A closer look can reveal the shape of its leaves, where its branches begin, or insects on its bark. Listening may reveal a bird you cannot see.
Looking carefully is a skill. Like any skill, it gets better with practice.
Practise looking closely in the investigation below. Tables 2.1 and 2.2 show possible records; your own entries may be different.
You will need: a notebook, a pencil, a water bottle.
Before the visit, copy the headings of Tables 2.1 and 2.2 into your notebook. Leave room for your own rows.
With your teacher, spend one period in a garden, park or school ground. Record the place, date and time.
Walk slowly, then stop at a safe place. Stand still and listen for thirty seconds. What different sounds can you hear?
Add a row for each kind of plant or animal you observe. If you do not know its name, describe or sketch it. For example: "small plant, three leaves together, near the tap".
Record only what you can establish. Write "not seen" for a feature you looked for but did not see. Do not pluck leaves or flowers or disturb animals.
Compare your records with a partner. Which living things were difficult to find or describe? What made them difficult?
Safety: Stay with your group. Do not touch any animal. Do not put your fingers into holes or under stones.

Separate what you saw from what you infer. The crow was seen on a wall and in a tree; that does not tell us every place it lives. "Pecking at something" does not identify its food. What further observation could help?
The variety of living things found in one region is called its biodiversity.
Your school ground has its own biodiversity. So does a pond. So does a forest, a seashore, and even the soil in a flowerpot.
Your search lasted one period. Name two kinds of living things that your method might have missed. Plan one change to the time, place or method that could help you find them.
Living Things Need Each Other
The living things in a place are not just sharing space. They are joined to each other.

A tree can provide shade for smaller plants and nesting places for birds. Some birds feed on insects on its bark. A fruit-eating bird may carry a seed away; the seed can grow if it reaches suitable conditions. Fallen leaves provide food for decomposers, which help return nutrients to the soil.
Removing a tree can remove shade, nest sites and a source of fallen leaves. The effects depend on which organisms use it and what other resources are available nearby.

Choose one plant or animal from your own record. Draw it in the centre of a notebook page. Add other living things it may depend on, or that may depend on it. Use arrows labelled "food", "shelter" or another relationship. Mark each link as observed, read about, or still a guess. Compare your diagram with a partner. Choose one uncertain link and suggest how you could check it. If one organism disappeared from your diagram, which links would be affected? Could another organism supply the same resource? Explain what you know and what you would need to find out.
2.2 Making Sense of the Variety
Your records may contain many kinds of living things. Grouping them can help you compare a feature without searching through every entry.
In a stationery shop, keeping pens together helps a customer find a pen. Arranging goods by price answers a different question: what can I buy with this amount of money?
Scientists do the same with living things. Putting things into groups by the features they share is called grouping.
You will need: old magazines or newspapers, scissors, glue, small cards.
Cut out pictures of plants and animals. Paste one on each card. Try to make at least thirty cards in the class.
Work in groups of five or six. Put all your cards together.
Sort the pile into groups. You decide what the groups will be.
Write down, in one line, the rule you used.
Now mix all the cards again. Sort them a second time, using a completely different rule.
Compare both your sortings with another group's.
Did any two groups in the class use the same rule?
Safety: Use scissors carefully, with your teacher’s guidance.
A Grouping Needs a Clear Rule
Take one sorted group and check every card against its rule. Two different rules can both be useful, but a card can still be placed incorrectly.
Different groups may use size, food or surroundings. Check what the pictures actually show before using these features.

How would a library arranged by book size help a reader? What would be harder to find?
2.2.1 Grouping Plants
Look at Table 2.1 again. The features you wrote there — stem, leaves, flowers — are the same features we can use to sort plants.
Begin with stems: their firmness, whether they are woody, and where they branch. Examine plants your teacher says are safe to handle.
Go out to the same place as before. Choose six plants of clearly different sizes.
Stand next to each one. Is it shorter than you, about your height, or taller?
Look at the stem near the ground. Is it green or brown?
Bend the stem very gently with one finger. Does it bend, or is it stiff? Stop as soon as you feel it resist. A broken stem can kill the plant.
See where the branches start. Near the ground, or higher up?
Record these features using the headings in Table 2.3. Group your plants by shared stem features and explain your rule.
Did height and stem features give you the same groups? Which plants were difficult to place?

Compare your records with the descriptions below. Your sample may not contain all three forms, and young or pruned plants may be harder to classify.

blocks.html: Trees are woody plants that usually develop a main trunk supporting a crown of branches. Mango is an example. A young mango is still a tree even when it is shorter than a mature tomato plant.
Shrubs are woody plants that usually branch close to the ground, often with several main stems. A rose bush is an example. Observe the branching as well as the height.
Plants with soft, non-woody stems are called herbs. Many are small, such as mint, coriander and tomato, but height alone does not define a herb.
Woody stems support branches and can thicken as a plant grows. Look at the base of a tree and then a herb: what differences can you describe without damaging either?
A banana plant is a large herb. Its trunk-like structure is a pseudostem, made from tightly overlapping leaf bases rather than a woody trunk. Its height does not make it a tree.
Plants That Cannot Stand Up
Not every plant can hold itself up.

art.svg: <svg class="g6-source-art" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="80.9999980630239 327.0001709882363 889.9999926380066 371.8907603656862"><image class="science-illustration" href="../../figures/class-6/science/ch02/climbers.png" x="89" y="335" width="874" height="325" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet" data-original-bounds="{"x": 88.9999980630239, "y": 335.0001709882363, "w": 873.9999926380066, "h": 324.9996399747688}"/><text class="se-caption" x="363.87185354691076" y="685" text-anchor="middle" data-original-bounds="{"x": 275.980499949416, "y": 667.3274453217618, "w": 176.73452725671223, "h": 23.563486032160654}">Climber · grape vine</text><text class="se-caption" x="688.1281464530892" y="685" text-anchor="middle" data-original-bounds="{"x": 607.5773703956668, "y": 667.3274453217618, "w": 161.10161890236952, "h": 23.563486032160654}">Creeper · pumpkin</text></svg>

blocks.html: Some plants have stems that are too weak to stand. So they climb up something else — a wall, a fence, a stick, or another plant. These are called climbers. A money plant is a climber. So is a grape vine.
Other plants also have weak stems. But instead of climbing, they spread flat along the ground. These are called creepers. Pumpkin and watermelon plants are creepers.

Climbing and trailing describe growth habits, not a separate woody/non-woody division. A grape vine is a woody climber; a pumpkin has non-woody trailing stems. A plant can therefore be described in more than one way.
A climber and a creeper both have stems that need support or spread along the ground. What observations would you need before deciding which receives more light?
So far you have grouped plants using only the stem. Leaves give us another way to sort the same plants. We can compare these groups with the stem groups.
Lines on a Leaf
Hold a leaf up against the light. You will see thin lines running through it. These lines are veins. The pattern the veins make is called venation.
Veins contain tissues that transport water and dissolved substances. They carry water into the leaf and sugars made in the leaf to other parts of the plant. They also help support the leaf.
You will need: fallen leaves of at least four different plants, thin paper, a pencil with soft lead.
Put a leaf on the desk with its back side facing up. The veins stand out more on that side.
Place a sheet of thin paper over the leaf.
Hold the paper still. Rub the side of the pencil lead flat across it, using light strokes.
Check the print against the leaf. If the veins are unclear, adjust the paper or pressure and try again.
Do this for every leaf. Write the plant's name next to each print.
Put all your prints side by side.
Group the prints by their vein patterns. How many groups does your sample support? Explain your rule. If all the patterns look alike, compare with another group’s leaves.

A rubbing is a record made by a method. A faint patch may mean the paper moved or the pencil missed it. Check that patch on the actual leaf before describing its veins. Keep an unclear print beside your improved one so you can explain why you changed the record.

Compare the vein pattern separately from the leaf outline. Two leaves can have different outlines yet share a vein pattern. Point to the lines that support your grouping; another group should be able to follow your rule without knowing the plant names.
Two Patterns
Compare your prints with these examples. Two common patterns are shown here; your sample may contain only one.

blocks.html: In reticulate venation, veins branch to form a net. A thick middle vein is visible in the hibiscus leaf; finer veins branch and join around it. Mango, neem and peepal also have net-like venation.

In other leaves, many veins run alongside one another. This pattern is called parallel venation. In a grass blade they run along the length of the leaf. A banana leaf has a strong middle vein, with many parallel side veins running out towards its edges. Parallel venation does not mean that a leaf has no middle vein.
These two patterns help you compare many of the leaves around you. Look closely: real leaves sometimes show exceptions.
Predict the venation of wheat or maize from the examples. Then inspect a leaf or a clear photograph. Was your prediction supported? Leaf shape alone is not proof of its vein pattern.
Leaves are only part of the comparison. Next, examine roots.
Under the Ground
Roots hold plants in place and take up water and dissolved minerals. You can observe their growth as seeds germinate.
You will need: a handful of chana (chickpea) seeds, a handful of wheat seeds, two shallow trays or plates, cotton cloth or cotton wool, water.
Soak both kinds of seed in water overnight.
Spread a wet cloth in each tray. Put the chana seeds in one tray. Put the wheat seeds in the other.
Keep both trays in the same place. Keep the cloth damp, not flooded, and check it every morning for six days.
From day three, inspect the seedlings daily. Record when each germinates and sketch the roots without tearing them.
On day six, compare several seedlings of each kind. Keep any that germinated late and observe them for a few more days. Do not pull roots out of the cloth; examine them gently.
Draw what grew from each kind of seed in your notebook. Use the same scale for both drawings.
Could drawings alone tell you which plant is harder to pull out? What would you need to keep alike in a comparison of root anchorage?

Give each seedling a small identifying label and date each sketch. This lets you follow one seedling through time instead of mistaking differences between seedlings for changes in one plant. Place a ruler beside it without disturbing the roots; include a scale in your drawing.

Count age from germination as well as recording the calendar date. If one seed germinated on Monday and another on Thursday, drawings made on Friday show different stages of growth. Compare seedlings of similar age before deciding that a difference belongs to the two kinds of plant.
Two Kinds of Root
Compare several seedlings of each kind. Did they germinate at the same time? Root systems change as seedlings develop, so record the age as well as the shape.

blocks.html: A chana seedling usually develops one main root with smaller side roots. A main root of this kind is a taproot. Mustard and radish also develop taproots. The enlarged edible part of a radish includes a swollen taproot that stores food.

As the wheat seedling develops, several thin roots appear. Later, more roots grow from the base of the stem, forming a spreading bunch without one dominant main root. These are called fibrous roots. Grass, maize and lemongrass have them.
Both root systems anchor plants and take up water and dissolved minerals. Their branching patterns differ; their jobs overlap.
A taproot can grow deep and reach water below the surface. A deep root system can help a plant through a dry spell, although root depth also depends on the species and the soil.
Many fibrous root systems spread through the upper soil. A dense network helps hold loose soil together and take up water near the surface. Some fibrous roots also reach deep into the ground.
A Pattern Appears
You now know two ways to sort plants. One uses leaves. One uses roots.
Can a record of leaf venation help you predict root type? First collect observations, then test any pattern against another plant.
With your teacher or gardener, select five kinds of flowering plants with developed leaves and visible roots. Use spare nursery plants, not plants pulled from the wild.
Make a notebook table using the headings in Table 2.4. Examine four kinds first and record their venation and root type. Mark unclear features as uncertain.
Look for a connection in these four records. Use it to predict the root type of the fifth kind from its leaf. Record the prediction before examining its roots.
Check the roots of the fifth kind. Does this new observation support your proposed pattern? Compare results across the class.
Handle the roots gently and replant the plants with your teacher’s help.

blocks.caption: Table 2.4 · Leaf venation and root type

blocks.html: What happened with the fifth plant? An unclear root or leaf is a reason to examine it again, not to change the record so it fits.
The Two Go Together
Pool the class records. Count how many support a connection and how many do not. Compare the result with these common patterns in flowering plants.
Many familiar flowering plants with reticulate venation develop taproots; those with parallel venation commonly develop fibrous root systems.
Sadabahar has net-like veins and a taproot. Chana has net-like veins and a taproot. Lemongrass has parallel veins and fibrous roots. Wheat has parallel veins and fibrous roots.
These are typical associations, not rules without exceptions. Age, how a plant was propagated, and unusual features can affect what you observe. Keep exceptions in the record.
Could another feature help us recognise these groups? Look inside a seed.
Soak a few chana seeds and a few maize seeds in water for two days, until they are soft and swollen.
Peel the thin outer coat off a soaked chana. Now try to split the seed with your thumbnail.
Try gently to separate a soaked maize grain. Do not use a knife or force it apart. Record what you can see; compare with the labelled section afterwards.
Which seed comes apart neatly into two halves? Which one does not?
What Is Inside a Seed

A soaked chana can separate into two fleshy seed leaves called cotyledons. They store food for the young plant. Between them is the rest of the embryo, including a tiny root and shoot. Compare your specimen with the labelled illustration. Trace each label to the part it names, then locate that part in your specimen if it is visible.

In maize, one thin cotyledon lies beside the embryo’s tiny shoot and root. The larger pale region is stored food called the endosperm; it is not a second cotyledon. Failure to split the grain is not itself proof of the cotyledon count.
Cotyledon number, leaf venation and root type are associated features. The comparison does not show that cotyledon number causes the other two.
Among flowering plants, those whose seeds have two cotyledons are called dicotyledons. We say dicots for short. Plants whose seeds have one cotyledon are called monocotyledons, or monocots.

A prediction belongs in a separate column until you can inspect an intact root system. Otherwise, the table would seem to confirm an idea that you had not actually tested.
2.2.2 Grouping Animals
Animals vary as much as plants do. So the same question comes up. Which feature should we use to group them?
Colour or size may be useful for some questions. To compare movement, we need to record how an animal moves and which body parts it uses.
Use your animal records as a starting point. Add observations from direct watching or a reliable video, and identify which source you used.
Choose four animals you can safely watch or observe in a reliable video. Include one that moves in more than one way.
For each one, write how it moves and which body part it uses.
Use Table 2.5 as a guide for your notebook table.
Group your animals using the body parts you observed in use. Allow a record to appear in more than one group if your rule requires it.

blocks.caption: Table 2.5 · How animals move

blocks.html: A pigeon walks and flies. How would you record it in a grouping by body parts used for movement? Would forcing every animal into only one group lose information? Explain with your records.
What Movement Tells Us
Animals move in many ways. They walk, run, hop, crawl, fly, swim and glide. Some do more than one, like a pigeon.

Sorting them this way shows us something interesting. Animals that are not alike at all may still move in the same way, using similar body parts. A housefly and a pigeon are very different creatures. But both have wings, and both fly. A fish and a dolphin look alike in water, even though a dolphin is not a fish.
That is a clue about something you will meet soon in this chapter. The way an animal is built has a lot to do with where it lives.

Movement is not the only way to group animals. We can also group them by what they eat, by where they live, or by what covers the body — scales, feathers, fur, or exposed skin. As with plants, the best grouping depends on the question we are asking.
Know a scientist

Janaki Ammal (1897–1984) was one of the first Indian women to work as a professional botanist. She studied sugarcane and worked on making plant varieties better. In 1952 she became Officer on Special Duty at the Botanical Survey of India and helped reorganise its work. In her eighties she joined the fight to save the forest at Silent Valley in Kerala. Her whole life was spent doing the two things this chapter is about — looking closely at plants, and finding order in what she saw.

Built for the Place

blocks.html: Look at a plant from a hot desert.

Consider a cactus adapted to a hot, dry habitat. Its fleshy stem stores water and its waxy surface reduces water loss. In many cacti, leaves are reduced to spines and the green stem carries out photosynthesis.
Now look at a deodar tree, high in the Himalayas.
On snowy mountain slopes, snow can load branches heavily. The conical form and sloping branches of a deodar can help shed snow. Temperature, soil and water also affect where a tree can grow.
These features were not chosen by individual plants. They are inherited features found in populations living in particular conditions. Other plants may survive there using different features.

Suppose a cactus from a frost-free desert is moved to a place with freezing winters and persistently wet soil. Which new conditions would you investigate before deciding whether it could survive? The word "mountain" alone is not enough information.
Two Camels, Two Deserts
Compare the two kinds of camel in the illustration. Which visible differences could matter in cold weather?

Camels live in the hot sandy desert of Rajasthan. Camels also live in the cold, high, rocky desert of Ladakh. Both places are deserts. Both are dry, with little food and little shelter. But they are dry in very different ways. And the two camels are not the same.

blocks.html: The Rajasthan camel is tall, with long legs. Its two-toed feet have broad, spreading pads. They spread its weight, so it does not sink into loose sand. It has one hump. Its coat is thin.

The Ladakh camel is shorter and heavier. Its sturdy legs also end in broad, padded, two-toed feet. It has two humps. It grows a thick shaggy coat, especially at the head and neck, for winters that fall far below freezing.

You may have heard that a camel stores water in its hump. That is not true. The hump stores fat. The camel lives off that fat when there is no food. When a camel uses much of this stored fat, its humps can become smaller and less upright.

Camels save water in other ways. They pass very little urine. Their dung is dry enough to burn. They can allow their body temperature to rise during the day, reducing the water needed for cooling. They do sweat when necessary. How long a camel can go without drinking depends on heat, activity and the food available.
Adaptations
The cactus stem, the deodar's sloping branches, the camel's padded feet and hump — all of these are examples of one idea.
How It Works

Inherited features that help organisms survive and reproduce in their usual environment are called adaptations. They develop in populations over generations; an individual does not acquire a needed feature simply by trying.

Adaptations are not always about extreme places, and they are not always easy to spot. A fish has a smooth body that slips through water easily, and fins to steer and push with. A duck has skin joining its toes. That turns each foot into a paddle. A pigeon's toes are not joined by broad webbing. Its separate toes help it grip supports and walk.

Rhododendrons include low shrubs and tall trees in different mountain regions. Their features reflect both inherited differences and growing conditions. Even plants of the same species may grow differently in a windy, exposed place and in a sheltered one. A change in one plant's growth is not the same as an inherited adaptation developing over generations.
Two plants of the same species grow in different places, one windy and one sheltered. If their heights differ, what other factors would you check before attributing the difference to wind?

blocks.html: Habitat
The place where a living thing lives is called its habitat.

A habitat includes the conditions and resources an organism uses. Plants need light, water and minerals; animals need food as well as suitable conditions. A habitat need not be safe at all times, and an animal may use different places to feed or breed.
A habitat can be small: damp soil beneath a fallen log differs from the dry path beside it. Such differences help explain why nearby places can hold different living things.
Habitats can be sorted into two broad kinds.
Living things on land live in terrestrial habitats. Forests, deserts, grasslands and mountains are terrestrial habitats. So is the ground under your feet.
Living things in water live in aquatic habitats. Ponds, lakes, rivers and oceans are aquatic habitats.

Some animals use both land and water. Frogs belong to a group called amphibians; many amphibians spend part of their lives in each. But using both habitats does not make every animal an amphibian. A crocodile does so too, and it is a reptile.
When a Habitat Is Lost
Ask your parents, your grandparents, or an older neighbour one simple question. Which birds, insects or plants did they see often as children, but rarely see now?
Record what the person remembers and where they lived. Memory is a starting point for a question, not proof of a change in population. Look for dated records or photographs to compare.

Habitat damage can reduce food, shelter or breeding sites. Some organisms may move; others may not be able to reach suitable places. Populations can decline or disappear locally. To investigate a decline, check both changes in habitat and how the observations were made.
Know a scientist

Salim Ali (1896–1987) spent many years travelling across India, watching birds. He recorded where they lived, when they arrived, and where they went next. Watching carefully like this, year after year, is how scattered sightings turn into real knowledge. His fieldwork and advocacy helped strengthen bird conservation in India. His books also made it possible for ordinary people to name the birds around them. He is remembered as the Birdman of India.
Protecting habitats

Habitat loss has threatened animals such as the Bengal tiger and the Great Indian bustard. Project Tiger began in 1973 to protect tigers and their habitats. The cheetah was declared extinct in India in 1952; a reintroduction programme began in 2022. Protecting suitable habitat is essential to conservation.

Checking Whether Protection Helps
Suppose a class records more kinds of birds in a protected grove than in a nearby clearing. Does that record alone show that protection caused the difference?
Check how the records were made. Were both places watched for the same length of time, at similar times of day? Could differences in area, water or vegetation also matter?
Plan repeated visits using the same method. Decide what to record so another class could check your comparison. A useful conclusion must account for both the evidence and its limits.
Keywords
Adaptation — An inherited feature that helps an organism survive and reproduce in its usual environment.
Amphibian — An animal belonging to the group that includes frogs and toads; many use water and land during their lives.
Aquatic — Living in water, or describing a habitat in water.
Biodiversity — The variety of living things found in a region.
Climber — A plant that grows upwards using external support.
Cotyledon — A seed leaf that is part of the embryo inside a seed.
Creeper — A plant with stems that trail along the ground.
Dicot — A flowering plant whose seed has two cotyledons.
Endosperm — Food-storing tissue in a seed that nourishes the developing embryo.
Fibrous root system — A spreading bunch of roots without one dominant main root.
Grouping — Arranging things by features they share, using a stated rule.
Habitat — The place where an organism lives, including its conditions and resources.
Herb — A plant with soft, non-woody stems; it need not be small.
Monocot — A flowering plant whose seed has one cotyledon.
Parallel venation — A leaf-vein pattern in which many veins run alongside one another.
Pseudostem — A trunk-like structure formed by overlapping leaf bases, as in banana.
Reticulate venation — A leaf-vein pattern in which veins branch and join to form a network.
Sacred grove — A patch of vegetation protected through local cultural or religious traditions.
Shrub — A woody plant that usually branches near the ground, often with several main stems.
Taproot — The main root of a root system, with smaller roots branching from it.
Terrestrial — Living on land, or describing a habitat on land.
Tree — A woody plant that usually develops a main trunk supporting a crown of branches.
Venation — The pattern of veins in a leaf.
Summary
• The variety of living things found in a region is called its biodiversity. Even an ordinary place has much more of it than a quick look suggests.
• Living things in a place depend on each other for food, shelter and other needs.
• Grouping means arranging things by the features they share. Different rules answer different questions; each must be applied consistently.
• Woody stems and branching help distinguish trees and shrubs from non-woody herbs. Climbing and trailing describe growth habits, which can overlap with these descriptions.
• The pattern of veins in a leaf is called venation. Two common patterns are reticulate and parallel.
• Two common root systems are taproot and fibrous root systems. A taproot has one main root. Fibrous roots form a spreading bunch.
• Among flowering plants, dicots have two cotyledons and monocots have one.

• These three features go together. Dicots generally have reticulate venation and a taproot. Monocots generally have parallel venation and fibrous roots. These associations support predictions that must be checked.
• Animals can be grouped by how they move and which body parts they use. They can also be grouped in many other ways.
• Adaptations are inherited features that help organisms survive and reproduce. They develop in populations over generations, not because an individual tries to change.
• The place where a living thing lives is its habitat. Habitats are terrestrial or aquatic. Many amphibians use both land and water, but not all animals that do so are amphibians.
• Damage to habitats causes loss of biodiversity. This is why habitats are protected — by governments, and by communities.

• Walk around your school with your teacher or the gardener. Label the plants with their local names. Make a list in your notebook. For each plant, record whether its stems are woody and how it grows: upright, climbing or trailing. Use herb, shrub or tree where the evidence supports it; more than one description can apply.

• Over one term, build a class biodiversity register. Revisit the same places for the same length of time. Record dates, weather and how you searched. • Interview an older person about local plants and animals. Ask where and when they saw them. Compare one recollection with a dated photograph, written record or another account. Identify what remains uncertain.

• Read about one Indian scientist working on biodiversity today. Write a short report. You could start with Divya Mudappa, Vidya Athreya, Uma Ramakrishnan, Nandini Velho, Ghazala Shahabuddin, Usha Lachungpa or Divya Karnad.

The bell for lunch break rings at Meridian Public School, and within a minute the corridor smells of six different homes. Aarav opens his tiffin — lemon rice, still warm. Ira opens hers — two rotis and a bowl of dal. From the next bench comes the smell of fish curry, from the bench behind, of dhokla.
Aarav looks around the room: the lunches differ. Which ingredients do they share, and what does the body obtain from them?
So what is actually happening inside all those tiffin boxes? Why does food make us able to run, and think, and grow?
Look at your own lunch today. Name three things in it. Where did each one come from?
3.1 What Do We Eat in a Week?
Aarav's question is a good one, and the honest answer is that we cannot say much about food in general until we look at food in particular. So begin with the food you know best: your own.

Most of us eat without paying attention. We eat what is served, at the time it is served, and we rarely notice the pattern. But there is pattern. Over a week, your meals repeat, vary, and cluster in ways that tell you something about your household, your region, and your health.

Scientists call this kind of careful watching observation. Observation is not the same as looking. Looking is what you do all day. Observing is looking with a question in mind, and writing down what you find.
You will need: your notebook, seven days.
Create a food diary in your notebook, with one entry for each day.
Every evening for one week, write down everything you ate that day — meals, snacks, drinks, everything. Do not leave out the biscuit you ate at 4 p.m.
Write it the same evening. If you wait till Sunday and try to remember Monday, you may forget or misremember items; mark any uncertain entries.
At the end of the week, read the whole table at once.

Follow the Evidence
The examples link wheat with Punjabi dishes, ragi with dishes in Karnataka, and rice with dishes in Manipur. Is the same relationship present in your other rows? Look for an exception as well.
Local crops can influence food traditions, but proximity alone does not guarantee the cheapest or freshest food. Transport, storage, season and farming costs also matter.
How It Works

Soil, rainfall and temperature affect which crops grow well. Rice is often grown in flooded fields, though not all rice requires standing water. Ragi can tolerate relatively dry conditions. Farmers can also change irrigation and soil management.

Soil and climate are not the whole story. Culture, religion and history all shape what a community eats and what it avoids. Two families in the same street, growing food from the same fields, may cook very differently.
Follow the Evidence
Regional food reflects crops, trade, cost, taste, culture and tradition. A crops-and-dishes table suggests relationships; it does not isolate a single cause.
Choose a dish common in your state. Is it also eaten across the border? Check with two sources before explaining any difference using crops, trade or tradition.
3.1.2 Food also varies from time to time

Food varies across the map. Does it also vary across the years? Interview an older person about dishes, fuel and cooking tools. Record continuity as well as change; one memory cannot represent every household.
Choose someone at least fifty years older than you — a grandparent, a neighbour, a retired teacher.

Prepare your questions before you meet them. Write them down. Good starting points: What did you eat as a child that you still eat today? What did you eat then that you never eat now? How was the food cooked, and on what? How long did the cooking take? What changed, and when did it change?
Listen more than you talk. Write their answers in their words, not yours.
Bring your notes to class and pool them with your classmates'.

blocks.html: Pool the class's interview notes and a shared picture appears. The way food is prepared — what we can call culinary practice — has changed sharply within living memory.

A chulha burns fuel such as wood or dung cakes; a gas stove burns gas. A sil-batta grinds food by hand; a mixer-grinder uses an electric motor. These tools coexist today. Your interviews can show which changes occurred in particular homes and when.
Why did all this change?
Partly because the technology arrived. Gas connections, electricity and affordable appliances reached ordinary households, and once a tool that saves an hour a day is available, people use it.

Partly because transport improved. Roads, railways and cold storage mean that a fruit grown in Himachal can be sold in Chennai. Foods that were once purely local became available everywhere, and cuisines began to borrow from each other.
Television, phones and the internet can spread recipes beyond a region. To test a claim about how quickly one dish spread, we would need dated evidence from several places.

Change of this kind brings real gains. Cooking takes less time — which matters most to the women who have historically done most of it. Fuel-efficient stoves mean less smoke indoors, and less smoke means healthier lungs.

Changes can also reduce the use of familiar grains or cooking skills. Whether a replacement is more nourishing depends on its ingredients, preparation and quantity. Compare examples rather than assuming that older or newer food is better.

Smoke in the kitchen A wood or dung chulha burning indoors fills a kitchen with fine smoke. Breathing that smoke for years damages the lungs and the heart, and the person standing closest to the stove breathes the most of it. This is one reason governments have worked to bring clean cooking fuel to rural households: a better stove is a health measure, not just a convenience.
3.2 What Is Food Made Of?
Aarav misses breakfast and feels hungry during class. Ira shares a banana at break. Later he says he feels better.
Does that observation prove what caused the change? Rest, water and other factors may matter too. We need knowledge of digestion to explain what food can supply; this story is not a blood-sugar test.

Something in food, then, is not the same as food. When we eat a banana we are not eating "banana" as far as the body is concerned. We are eating a mixture of substances, each of which the body uses for a different job. These substances are the components of food.
Different foods carry different components in different amounts. That is why no single food keeps a person well, and why the mixture on the plate matters as much as the items on it.
Begin with carbohydrates, one group of food components.
Carbohydrates
How It Works

Glucose is a simple sugar and a carbohydrate. Cells can release energy from glucose. Starch is also a carbohydrate; digestion breaks it down into smaller sugars before absorption. Foods supply mixtures, so a banana is not a dose of pure glucose.

We rarely eat pure glucose. We eat carbohydrates in the form of cereals — wheat, rice, maize, jowar; in root vegetables — potato and sweet potato; and in fruits — banana, mango, pineapple, sugarcane. Ordinary table sugar is a carbohydrate too.

blocks.html: Fats
How It Works

Ghee and cooking oils contain fats. Fat supplies about twice as much energy per gram as carbohydrate. The body can use fat for energy or store it; it does not automatically store all dietary fat. Stored fat also cushions organs and reduces heat loss. These functions do not establish a special need for laddoos in winter.

Fats come from plants and from animals. Plant sources include groundnut, walnut, cashew, almond, pistachio, coconut, sesame seed, pumpkin seed, sunflower seed, soya bean and the oils pressed from them. Animal sources include butter, ghee, curd and milk.

blocks.html: Stored fat in a polar bear: pregnant females can spend months in a den without feeding, drawing on stored reserves while giving birth and nursing cubs. Most other polar bears remain active and hunt through winter. Fat also provides insulation.
Name three foods you ate this week that contained a visible fat. Where did each fat come from — a plant or an animal?
Proteins

Carbohydrates and fats supply energy, and fats also form parts of cells. Proteins have an essential role in building and repairing tissues. These job labels overlap; they are not exclusive compartments.

Consider what a body has to do besides move. A six-year-old grows into a sixteen-year-old. A cut on your hand closes over in a week. Hair grows, nails grow, muscle thickens with training. All of that is construction work, and construction needs material.
The material is protein.
How It Works

Proteins are used to build new tissue and repair damaged tissue. This is why the diet of a growing child must contain enough protein, and why an athlete training for strength needs more than a person who is not. A body short of protein cannot grow properly, however much energy it is given — you cannot build a wall out of firewood.

Pulses, soya beans, nuts and seeds supply protein. Milk, curd, paneer, eggs, fish and meat are other sources. Compare amounts as well as presence: fresh mushrooms contain protein but are mostly water and supply less per usual serving than pulses.
Because of the job they do, protein-rich foods are called body-building foods — while carbohydrates and fats, which supply energy, are together called energy-giving foods.

Mushrooms belong to the fungi, not the plants. They obtain nutrients from organic matter rather than making sugars by photosynthesis. Fresh edible mushrooms contain water, fibre and nutrients, but are not interchangeable with pulses as a protein source. Never taste a wild mushroom to identify it.
3.3 The Components We Need in Tiny Amounts

Carbohydrates, fats and proteins are the components we eat by the spoonful. There is another set that we need in amounts so small they are measured in milligrams — and yet a person who goes without them falls seriously ill.
The strongest way to see what these components do is to look at what happens when they are missing. Read the two cases below and work out the answer yourself before reading on.
Case 1 — The sailors' disease

On long sea voyages in earlier centuries, sailors fell ill in a particular way. Their gums swelled and bled, their teeth loosened, old wounds reopened, and many died — often months from any battle or storm.
In May 1747, James Lind compared six treatments among twelve sailors with scurvy, two sailors per treatment. The pair receiving oranges and lemons improved most rapidly.
The condition is called scurvy.

Now interpret Case 1. Lind's sailors were not short of food — ships carried salted meat and dry biscuit in quantity. They were short of something present in lemons and oranges and absent from salted meat.

That something is now called Vitamin C. Scurvy is caused by a lack of Vitamin C in the diet, and it is prevented and cured by foods that contain it — citrus fruits like lemon and orange, and also amla, guava and green chilli.
Follow the Evidence

The comparison supplied evidence favouring citrus fruit over the other treatments tested. It did not identify Vitamin C, and two sailors per treatment is a small sample. More observations and later research were needed to establish the cause.
Lind's sailors ate plenty of food and still fell ill. What does that tell you about the difference between eating enough and eating well?
Case 2 — The swelling in the neck

In the 1960s, Indian scientists studying the Himalayan region and the northern plains found that a large number of people there had a visible swelling at the front of the neck. It was common in some districts and rare in others only a few hundred kilometres away.
Following the scientists' findings, the Government of India promoted the addition of iodine to common salt — iodised salt. Where people switched to it, the swellings became far less common.
The condition is called goitre.
How It Works

Iodine deficiency can enlarge the thyroid gland, causing goitre. Diets relying on crops from iodine-poor soil can contribute. But a neck swelling can have other causes: symptoms alone do not diagnose a nutrient deficiency.

Iodised salt is a way to supply a small, controlled amount of iodine through a widely used ingredient. This does not mean eating extra salt; it means using iodised salt within the usual limited amount.
You have probably read the words "iodised salt" on a packet without thinking about them. They mean common salt to which a small measured quantity of iodine salts has been added.
Vitamin C and iodine are examples of a larger group: the vitamins and minerals.

In the Little Rann of Kutch, Agariya salt workers pump underground brine into evaporation pans. Water evaporates and salt crystallises. This example connects a food ingredient to separation by evaporation and to the people who produce it.

Vitamin C and iodine are two of many. Each vitamin and each mineral has its own job, its own food sources, and its own set of symptoms when the body runs short. Together they are what keep the body's defences and daily processes working.
Fig. 3.5 sets out the main ones. Read it carefully — you will be using it again in the exercises at the end of the chapter.

blocks.title: Vitamin A
items: Papaya, carrot, mango, milk
What it does: Keeps eyes and skin healthy
Deficiency disorder: Loss of vision
Possible signs; not a diagnosis: Poor vision; loss of vision in dim light (night blindness); in severe cases, complete loss of vision

blocks.title: Vitamin B₁
items: Legumes, nuts, whole grains, seeds, milk products
What it does: Helps release energy from food and supports nerve function
Deficiency disorder: Beriberi
Possible signs; not a diagnosis: Swelling, tingling or burning in the feet and hands; difficulty in breathing

blocks.title: Vitamin C
items: Amla, guava, green chilli, orange, lemon
What it does: Needed to make collagen for connective tissues and wound healing
Deficiency disorder: Scurvy
Possible signs; not a diagnosis: Bleeding gums; wounds heal slowly

blocks.title: Vitamin D
items: Skin makes it in sunlight; oily fish, egg yolk, fortified milk
What it does: Helps the body absorb calcium for bones and teeth
Deficiency disorder: Rickets
Possible signs; not a diagnosis: Soft, bent bones

blocks.title: Calcium
items: Milk, curd, cheese, paneer; calcium-fortified soya milk
What it does: Keeps bones and teeth strong
Deficiency disorder: Poor bone mineralisation
Possible signs; not a diagnosis: Low intake over time can weaken bones; tooth decay has other causes

blocks.title: Iodine
items: Iodised salt, seafood, dairy and eggs; amounts vary
What it does: Needed to make thyroid hormones, supporting growth and development
Deficiency disorder: Goitre
Possible signs; not a diagnosis: Swelling at the front of the neck

blocks.title: Iron
items: Pulses, leafy greens, meat and iron-fortified foods; absorption varies
What it does: Part of haemoglobin, which carries oxygen in blood
Deficiency disorder: Anaemia
Possible signs; not a diagnosis: Weakness; shortness of breath

blocks.html: A nutrient is a substance the body needs for energy, growth, repair or normal functioning. Carbohydrates, fats, proteins, vitamins and minerals are nutrient groups; water is an essential nutrient too.

The labels energy-giving, body-building and protective highlight important functions, but the jobs overlap. Proteins can supply energy, fats form parts of cells, and vitamins and minerals support many processes.
Vitamins and minerals help body processes work normally. Calling them protective does not mean that eating one food prevents every disease or treats every symptom.

This is why you are told to drink milk, eat green vegetables, eat fruit, and eat whole grains rather than only polished ones — not because these foods are filling, but because they carry the nutrients that nothing else will supply.
Vitamin D is on the list, but one of its sources is not a food at all. Which one — and what does that tell you about spending time outdoors?
3.4 Cooking, Roughage and Water
Have you noticed that a raw carrot snaps and a boiled one bends? That spinach loses its bright green in the pan?

Heat changes food, and not only in ways we can see. Some nutrients — Vitamin C among them — are partly destroyed by high heat. Washing vegetables and fruit after cutting or peeling them washes some vitamins away as well.

Two sensible conclusions follow. First, include some fruit and raw vegetables in your diet so that not everything you eat has been through a hot pan. Second, wash produce before you cut it, not after.
But do wash it. Thoroughly, every time. The vitamins lost to washing are a small price against the dirt, pesticide residue and germs that washing removes.

Aarav: That's what the chapter says.
Ira: Then where does salt come from? Not a plant. Not an animal.
Aarav: Seawater. Or rock.
Ira: And Vitamin D — the teacher said our own skin makes it in sunlight. That isn't food either.
Two further components to consider are dietary fibre and water. Water is an essential nutrient even though it supplies no energy.

Dietary fibre, or roughage, comes mainly from plant foods such as whole grains, pulses, fruit and vegetables. Our own digestive enzymes do not break it down, although gut microbes can break down some fibre. Fibre helps bowel function; constipation can have several causes.

Water dissolves and transports substances, helps remove waste in urine and helps regulate temperature through sweating and evaporation. Needs vary with activity and weather. Water is a nutrient, not a source of food energy.
Which foods give you water besides water itself? List four.
Coluthur Gopalan (1918-2019)

To study diets in India, researchers needed reliable measurements of the foods people ate, along with records of amounts and preparation. A foreign food table could not represent every local ingredient or recipe.

Coluthur Gopalan set out to find out. Over his career he and his colleagues analysed the nutritional content of more than five hundred Indian foods — not foods from foreign tables, but the grains, pulses, vegetables and greens that Indian households actually cooked. It is difficult, unglamorous laboratory work, and it produced something India had never had: reliable numbers for its own diet.

He then led large surveys of what Indians were eating and how healthy they were. The surveys found widespread shortages of protein and energy, particularly among children — not in a few unlucky families, but across whole populations.

The national school nutrition programme began in 1995 and developed into the cooked school-meal programme now called PM POSHAN. Nutrition research helped shape school feeding policy. A programme date alone does not prove its effects: those require measurements of children and meals.
Gopalan died in 2019, aged 101.

3.5 How Do We Test for Nutrients?

So far you have taken this chapter's word for it. Time to check for yourself. Some nutrients need a well-equipped laboratory to detect. Three do not: starch, fat and protein can each be tested with equipment a school already has. Starch, incidentally, is a carbohydrate — the form in which plants store it.

Before each test, record what you expect and why. This is a prediction. Keep it beside the observation even if they disagree. Both matching and unexpected results matter; neither alone proves a complete explanation.
You will need: small samples of potato, cucumber, bread or chapati, boiled rice, boiled gram, crushed peanut, oil, butter, crushed coconut; a dropper; dilute iodine solution; separate dishes.
Use starch paste as a positive control and water as a negative control. Keep sample amounts and waiting times alike. Record observations before interpreting them.
Copy the results-table headings given below into your notebook. Fill in the prediction column before you touch the iodine.
Place a small piece of each food on its own dish. Keep them apart and label them.
Note the colour of each sample before testing.
Using the dropper, put two or three drops of dilute iodine solution on each sample.
Watch for a colour change. Record what you see.
Compare each sample with both controls. What changed? Did the controls behave as expected? What would you repeat before concluding absence?
How It Works
Iodine forms a blue-black complex with starch. Compare with the starch control: a matching change supports starch being present. A negative result cannot establish absence if the control failed.

blocks.html: You will need: the same food samples; plain paper.
Use cooking oil as a positive control and water as a negative control. Keep sample amounts and waiting times alike. Record observations before interpreting them.
Take a small piece of each food from the iodine investigation.
Place each on a separate piece of paper. Label the papers.
Fold the paper over the food and press firmly. Do not tear it.
If a food is watery, set the paper aside until it dries — a wet patch is not an oily patch, and confusing the two will ruin your result.
Hold each paper up to the light.
Compare each sample with both controls. What changed? Did the controls behave as expected? What would you repeat before concluding absence?
How It Works

Oil leaves paper translucent after water has evaporated. A persistent patch matching the oil control supports fat being present. A faint or absent patch can also depend on sample amount and transfer to the paper.

3.6 What Is a Balanced Diet?

Does everyone need the same food in the same amounts? Clearly not. A twelve-year-old is still growing and needs more protein for her size than her grandfather does. A farmhand doing heavy work all day needs more energy than someone at a desk. A person recovering from illness has different needs again. Requirements shift with age, sex, level of physical activity, state of health and way of life. A balanced diet is one that supplies all the nutrients a particular person needs, in the right amounts, together with enough roughage and water. Note the phrase a particular person. There is no single balanced diet for everybody — the idea only means anything once you say who is eating.

3.8 Millets: The Grains That Came Back

Jowar, bajra, ragi, sanwa, kodo, kutki — these are millets, and they are among the oldest cultivated grains in India. For centuries they were ordinary food across large parts of the country. Then, within a few decades, they largely disappeared from urban plates, pushed aside by polished rice and refined wheat.

blocks.caption: Fig. 3.9 · Sanwa (barnyard millet) growing in a field

blocks.html: Compare the grains by named nutrients and growing conditions. A single label such as healthy cannot replace those comparisons.

Millets are small-grained cereals, so they supply carbohydrate like any cereal. What sets them apart is what comes with the carbohydrate: substantially more dietary fibre than polished rice, along with iron, calcium and B vitamins. Because of this they are often called nutri-cereals — cereals that carry protective nutrients alongside energy.

Many millets tolerate relatively dry conditions and can need less irrigation than flooded rice. Water use still depends on crop, yield, climate and farming practice. Compare like growing conditions before making a numerical claim.
Millets can add variety and nutrients and can suit dry regions. This does not make every millet superior to every rice dish on every measure.
Would millets alone be enough?

No — and the reason is worth understanding. Millets are strong on carbohydrate, fibre and several minerals, but weak on some nutrients the body needs, and no cereal supplies everything. Eaten with dal, vegetables, milk or curd, millets make an excellent meal. Eaten alone, they leave gaps.
3.9 Food Miles: From the Field to the Plate

Aarav's lunch had rice in it. Ira's had wheat. Neither grew in the school. Follow a chapati backwards from the plate and you find a chain of work. A farmer prepares soil, sows wheat, waters and tends it for months, and harvests it. The grain is threshed and winnowed to separate it from the chaff. It is stored, often for months. It is transported to a mill and ground into flour. The flour is packed, transported again, and sold in a shop. Someone buys it, carries it home, kneads it, and cooks the chapati.
That is many months, many hands, and a great many kilometres, for one item on one plate.

3.10 Food We Throw Away
Now put the two ideas together.
Everything on your plate carries months of a farmer's work and a long journey behind it. Food left uneaten on the plate throws all of that away — the water, the labour, the fuel, the months.
The remedy is not complicated and needs no equipment. Take what you will eat. Go back for more if you are still hungry. Finish what you have taken.

KEYWORDS

Food and nutrition: carbohydrate fat protein • vitamin mineral nutrient protective nutrient • energy-giving food body-building food roughage balanced diet deficiency disorder scurvy rickets beriberi goitre anaemia iodised salt junk food millet nutri-cereal culinary practice cultivation food miles Ways of working: observe predict compare analyse infer interpret investigate survey correlate
Recap — the chapter in short

People across India eat widely different food, and the difference is not random. It follows the crops that grow in each region, which follow soil and climate, and is then shaped by culture, religion and taste.

Culinary practices have changed sharply within living memory — from chulha to gas stove, from sil-batta to mixer-grinder — driven by new technology, better transport and faster communication. The changes brought real gains and some real losses.
• Carbohydrates, fats, proteins, vitamins and minerals are nutrient groups studied here. Water is also an essential nutrient. Food supplies dietary fibre as well.
• Carbohydrates and fats supply energy and are called energy-giving foods. Fat carries more energy per gram than carbohydrate and is the body's store.
• Proteins build and repair the body and are called body-building foods. Growing children and athletes need proportionally more.

• Lack of a nutrient can cause a deficiency disorder. Symptoms can also have other causes, so medical assessment matters. Examples include Vitamin C deficiency causing scurvy and iodine deficiency contributing to goitre.
• Dietary fibre resists digestion by our own enzymes; gut microbes can break down some of it. Fibre helps bowel function. Water transports dissolved substances and helps regulate body temperature.

• Starch, fat and protein can be detected with simple tests: iodine turns starch blue-black, fat leaves a translucent oily patch on paper, and copper sulfate with caustic soda turns protein violet. Most foods contain more than one nutrient.
A balanced diet supplies all the nutrients a particular person needs, in the right amounts, with enough roughage and water. What is balanced depends on age, sex, activity, health and way of life.

• Junk foods carry plenty of energy from sugar and fat and little else. Millets are called nutri-cereals because they carry fibre and minerals along with their carbohydrate, and they grow on less water.
• Food miles measures distance, not total environmental impact. Transport method, farming and storage also matter. Wasted food wastes resources used to produce it.

Wild food near you. In many parts of India people gather uncultivated greens, fruit and mushrooms — the ranbhajis of Maharashtra are one example. find out whether anything is gathered wild near your town. Ask an older person; they will know things the internet does not.

• Write to your principal. With your classmates, list the junk foods most often eaten in your school. Then write a joint letter to your principal proposing which to remove from the canteen and what to offer instead. Cost your alternatives — a proposal nobody can afford will be refused.

blocks.html: Long ago, ships sailed from the coast of Kerala carrying pepper, cardamom and ginger. They went to lands far across the sea.
Those sailing ships had no engines, and finding a course across open water was difficult. So how did a sailor know which way to go?
By day, he watched the sun. By night, he watched the stars. Sailors learnt the night sky so well that they could tell their direction from it.
But now think about a storm. Thick clouds cover the sky for two days. There is no sun. There are no stars. There is water in every direction, and every direction looks the same.
Which way is home?
A naturally magnetic stone, supported so it could turn freely, offered a direction reference when the sky was hidden. A direction alone did not tell sailors their position or the route home.
This chapter is about that stone, and about the magnets we use today.
Magnets Around You
You have already met magnets many times, even if you did not notice them.
Hidden in Familiar Objects

Some pencil boxes shut with a soft click. A magnet is doing that. The duster on a writing board may stay stuck to the board. A magnet is doing that too. Fridge doors, cupboard doors, purses, toys, stickers — all of these may have magnets hidden in them.
A magnet produces a magnetic field: a region in which it can exert magnetic forces. It can attract iron and can attract or repel another magnet. A force may act even when friction prevents movement.

The first magnets were not made by people. They were found in the ground. Lodestone is naturally magnetised magnetite, an iron-containing mineral. A piece of lodestone pulls small bits of iron towards it. People discovered this a very long time ago.
Later, people learnt to make magnets from pieces of iron. Today magnets include steel magnets, ceramic ferrite magnets and magnets made from alloys containing neodymium.
The magnets in your school laboratory are made by people. So are the ones in pencil boxes and toys. All of these are artificial magnets.
Magnets are made in many shapes. Each shape suits a different job.
