blocks.html: Look around your classroom and your home. Where can you find a magnet doing a job?

A magnet’s shape gives a clue to its use. A long bar is easy to hold and turn. A ring can slide over a rod. Shape alone, however, does not tell you how strong a magnet is. Compare what the magnets can actually do.
4.1 Magnetic and Non-magnetic Materials
Bring a magnet near a steel pin and the pin jumps to it. Bring the same magnet near a rubber eraser and nothing happens.
So a magnet does not pull everything. It pulls only some things. Which ones?

You will need: a magnet, and many small objects made of different materials — a pencil, an eraser, a steel paper clip, a plastic scale, an iron nail, a glass marble, a coin, a piece of cloth, a key, a rubber band, a piece of wood, a sharpener.
Look at each object. Write down what material it is made of.
Now predict. Before you test anything, write down whether you think it will stick to the magnet. Write Yes or No for every object.
Only after all your predictions are written, bring the magnet near each object, one by one.
Write down what really happened.
Safety: Keep small magnets and objects away from young children. Never put a magnet in your mouth.
Compare the two columns. Where were you right? Where were you wrong? Look only at the objects that stuck. What do those objects have in common?

Test a part of the object whose material you know. A pencil may have a metal ferrule, and a sharpener may have a steel blade inside a plastic body. If only one part sticks, record that part rather than calling the whole object magnetic.

An object that does not stick may simply be too far from the magnet. Bring the magnet close without forcing the object against it. If a result surprises you, repeat the test and compare it with a known steel paper clip.
Copy these headings into your notebook and record your predictions and observations there.

blocks.caption: Table 4.1 · Which materials does a magnet pull?

blocks.html: Now read down the last two columns.
Some objects were pulled towards the magnet and stuck to it. Others showed no visible attraction in this test.
In these school tests, magnetic materials are materials, such as iron, that respond strongly enough to a magnet for us to notice the attraction. They need not already be permanent magnets.

Iron is a magnetic material. Steel is made mostly of iron. Many kinds of steel are magnetic, though some stainless steels are not. That is why a steel paper clip sticks. Two other metals, nickel and cobalt, are also magnetic. So are some mixtures of these metals with others.

We call materials with no noticeable response in these tests non-magnetic materials. This does not mean that every magnetic effect on them is exactly zero. Wood, rubber, plastic, glass, paper and cloth are all non-magnetic.
Here is something worth noticing. Not every metal is magnetic. Try a magnet on an aluminium vessel or a copper wire. Neither will stick. So "metal" and "magnetic" do not mean the same thing.
Which materials in your table were non-magnetic?

Coins and keys can give different results because they are made from different metals or mixtures. Test your own examples rather than guessing from their colour. A shiny surface does not tell you whether the material underneath is magnetic.
Compare two objects using the same magnet at the same distance. If you change both the object and the magnet, you cannot tell which change caused a different result.

A non-magnetic covering can hide a magnetic material. For example, a plastic-coated steel clip may still be attracted. This does not show that the plastic is magnetic; it shows that the magnet can act on the steel inside.
4.2 The Poles of a Magnet
Does a magnet pull equally hard everywhere along its length? Or are some parts stronger than others?

Iron filings are tiny bits of iron. Their pattern gives us evidence about the magnetic field. Keep the paper level and sprinkle a thin, even layer so that the starting arrangement does not decide the result.
You will need: iron filings, a sheet of paper, a bar magnet.
Place the bar magnet flat on the desk.
Cover it completely with the sheet of paper.
Sprinkle iron filings lightly over the paper, above the magnet.
Tap the paper gently a few times.
Watch where the filings gather.
Safety: Do not touch your eyes or breathe in iron filings. Keep them on the paper, collect them carefully and wash your hands afterwards.
Are the filings spread evenly? Or do they collect in some places more than others? What does this tell you about the magnet underneath?
Compare the pattern before and after gently tapping the paper. Tapping helps grains move; it does not create poles. Keep the amount of filings and the paper position the same.
Two Ends, Two Poles
The filings do not spread evenly. They gather in thick bunches at the two ends of the bar magnet. In the middle, there are hardly any.
How It Works
The pattern suggests a stronger effect near the ends. It is not a force meter: the filings become temporarily magnetised, turn into alignment and attract one another into chains.

The strongest regions near the ends are the poles of this bar magnet. The simple magnets studied here have a North and a South pole; specially made magnets may have several pole regions. One is called the North pole. The other is called the South pole. You will find out in a moment why those names were chosen.

A U-shaped magnet has poles at its two tips. In many school ring magnets, one flat face is North and the other is South. Pole positions depend on how a magnet is made; they need not look like the ends of a bar.

Now here is a question. Suppose you break a bar magnet in half. Would you get one piece with only a North pole, and another with only a South pole? You would not. Each broken piece turns out to be a complete magnet, with a North pole and a South pole of its own. Break those pieces again and the same thing happens. Cutting divides the material, not the two poles into separate objects. Each piece still has a North and a South pole. Do not break magnets to test this.

blocks.html: The letters N and S are a useful record of the poles. If the letters rub off, the poles remain. You can identify them again by comparing the magnet with a marked magnet or by letting it turn freely.
4.3 Finding Directions
We can now go back to the sailors in the storm.
You will need: a bar magnet, thread, a table or a stand, a sheet of paper.
Tie the thread around the middle of the bar magnet.
Hang it from the edge of a table, or from a stand. Move the thread a little until the magnet hangs level.
Make sure nothing made of iron or steel is nearby. Move away steel chairs, keys and pencil boxes.
Wait until the magnet stops turning on its own.
On the floor below, mark the spot under each end of the magnet. Join the two marks with a straight line.
Now give the magnet a gentle push so that it spins. Wait until it stops again.

blocks.html: Does it stop along the same line as before? Try it four or five times. Before you push it a sixth time, say out loud where it will stop.

Let the magnet turn without touching the table, floor or stand. A twisted thread can pull it away from its resting direction. If the result changes between trials, check the suspension and remove nearby magnetic objects before deciding that the magnet behaves differently.
Repeated observations are useful because one trial can be disturbed. Draw the line after each trial in your notebook and compare your records.
Always the Same Line
Compare your repeated trials. Does the same end return to the same direction? A sticking support or a nearby magnet can change the result.
Now find out what that line is. If you know where the sun rises, you know roughly where east is. Face east and stretch out your arms. North is on your left. South is on your right.
Away from nearby magnets and iron objects, it settles along the magnetic north-south line. This is usually close to geographic north-south, but not exactly the same.

One end always turns towards the north. That end is the North pole of the magnet. The other end always turns towards the south. That is the South pole. Now the names make sense. They are named after the direction each end looks for.
But why does this happen at all?
How It Works

Earth has a magnetic field. It exerts a turning effect, called torque, on a freely suspended magnet. The magnet rotates into alignment with the local field; it is not being carried towards the North Pole. Earth does not contain a giant bar magnet.

Repeat with an iron bar, if your teacher has one. Record its direction without prescribing a result. Iron can retain magnetisation, and its shape and Earth's field can affect alignment. Failure to turn is not proof that a bar is unmagnetised.

This gives us a useful test. Hang a metal bar freely. If the same end repeatedly points towards magnetic north, that is evidence that the bar is magnetised. Check that it turns freely and that no nearby magnet is disturbing it.

A compass direction is a local observation. Nearby iron and other magnets can change it. That is why checking the surroundings is part of the experiment, just as important as waiting for the magnet to stop.
The Magnetic Compass
A hanging magnet works, but it is not much use on a rolling ship. It needs to be small, steady, and easy to read.
That is exactly what a magnetic compass is.

Inside a compass there is a thin magnet shaped like a needle. The needle sits balanced on a sharp pin, so it can turn very easily. Under the needle is a dial with the directions marked on it. A clear cover keeps out wind and rain.

Leave the compass on a flat surface and wait. The needle swings and then settles along the north-south line, just as the hanging magnet did. The end that points north is usually painted red, or marked in some other way.

To read it, turn the whole compass box gently — not the needle — until the marked north-seeking end points to N on the dial. Matching only the needle's line could put the dial backwards. The dial now gives magnetic directions; these can differ from geographic directions.

This small device changed the world. With a compass, a ship could hold its course through cloud, fog and night. It supplied a direction reference; sailors still needed information about their position and planned route.

blocks.html: The compass needle turns; the letters printed on the dial do not. Turning the case brings those letters into line with the settled needle. If you carry the compass to another place or turn yourself around, let the needle settle and check the dial again.
A compass shows direction relative to the local magnetic field. Accurate map navigation also allows for the difference between magnetic north and geographic north.
Keep the compass level while reading it. A tilted needle may catch against its support or case. If it seems stuck, put the compass on a flat surface and wait before trusting the direction it shows.
Make Your Own Compass
You do not need to buy a compass. You can make one.
You will need: a steel sewing needle, a bar magnet, a small piece of cork, a bowl of water, a few steel pins.
Before stroking, test whether the needle attracts a pin. Record the result in your notebook, then lay the needle flat on a wooden table.
Hold one pole of the bar magnet at one end of the needle. Press lightly and slide it along the needle to the other end.
At the end of the needle, lift the magnet right up and away.
Bring the same pole back to the same starting end. Slide it along again in the same direction.
Repeat this thirty to forty times. Always stroke in one direction only. Always lift the magnet clear at the end of each stroke.
Put the bar magnet well away. Repeat the pin test and compare with your before-test. Attraction alone is not conclusive; check the floating needle next.
Ask an adult to secure the needle flat on top of the cork with a small piece of tape, so it stays level.
Float the cork in the bowl of water. The needle should stay above the water.
Wait for it to stop turning.
Safety: Sewing needles are sharp. Ask an adult to tape the needle to the cork. Keep its point away from hands.

<svg class="g6-source-art" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="648.0 922.0 299.0 238.24785124783193"><svg class="science-illustration ip-art" x="656" y="930" width="283" height="189.35724743777453" viewBox="85 58 1366 914" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet" data-original-bounds="{"x":638.3901987168283,"y":917.9835965285565,"w":318.2196006664741,"h":212.14616074414153}"><image href="../../figures/class-6/science/ch04/png/floating-compass.png" x="0" y="0" width="1536" height="1024"/></svg><text class="se-caption" x="797.5" y="1146.3572474377745" text-anchor="middle" data-original-bounds="{"x":691.2227390724269,"y":1128.6843652156713,"w":213.29892383091544,"h":23.563486032160654}">Float the needle on cork.</text></svg>

blocks.html: Gently turn the cork and let it settle several times. Does the same needle end return towards magnetic north, checked with a compass well away from the bowl? What evidence is stronger than pin attraction alone?
What Makes the Needle Work?
How It Works

The stroking magnet does not transfer a magnetic substance to the needle. Its field helps align small magnetic regions inside the steel. Some alignment remains after the magnet is removed. This is magnetisation.

Using one pole and repeating the same stroke encourages a consistent alignment. Thirty to forty strokes is a starting procedure, not a guaranteed threshold: the needle material and magnet strength affect the result.
A fish-shaped floating model can use the same principle. The drawing is a model, not evidence of how a historical instrument was built.

A liquid can slow down a turning magnet. The essential idea is to support the magnet so it can turn freely. A solid piece of iron will sink unless its shape or a floating support keeps it at the surface.

art.svg: <svg class="g6-source-art" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="81.0 804.0 890.0 325.8903034471223"><svg class="science-illustration ip-art" x="89" y="812" width="874" height="275" viewBox="67 101 1402 844" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet" data-original-bounds="{"x":275.76303945601046,"y":779.0907681551507,"w":500.4738761441963,"h":333.6497002006272}"><image href="../../figures/class-6/science/ch04/png/fish.png" x="0" y="0" width="1536" height="1024"/></svg><text class="se-caption" x="526" y="1116" text-anchor="middle" data-original-bounds="{"x":331.69330757387644,"y":1098.3268174149616,"w":389.3603954672919,"h":23.563486032160654}">A floating model demonstrates the principle.</text></svg>

blocks.html: Compare your bowl compass with a bought compass. Which part is magnetised? Which part supports it? How could you test whether either needle is sticking?

Notice that all three solve the same problem in the same way. A magnet is allowed to turn freely, and then it is left alone to find its own direction. The cork provides floating support; a pin provides a pivot. Liquid slows turning. The dial labels directions. These parts do different jobs.

Compare the two designs by asking the same questions: what is magnetised, what supports it, and what prevents it from turning freely? These questions explain why a floating needle fails if its cork touches the side of the bowl.
4.4 Pushing and Pulling
So far, magnets have pulled things towards them. Now let us see what a magnet does to another magnet.
You will need: two bar magnets with their poles marked, five or six round pencils, a flat table.
Call the magnets A and B.
Lay the round pencils side by side on the table. Rest magnet A across them, so it can roll easily.
Hold magnet B in your hand. Slowly bring one end of it near one end of magnet A. Do not let them touch.
Watch magnet A carefully. Which way does it move?
Now turn magnet B around. Bring its other end near the same end of magnet A.
Watch again.
Did magnet A move towards magnet B both times? Or did it move away one of those times? Look at the pole markings. What was different between the two tries?
How It Works

The round pencils reduce rubbing between magnet A and the table. Without them, the magnetic force might be present but too weak to overcome the friction. A magnet that does not move immediately has not necessarily stopped exerting a force.
Like Poles and Unlike Poles
Compare your observations with the pole markings.
When the North pole of one magnet faces the South pole of another, the two are pulled together. This pulling together is called attraction.
When two North poles face each other, they push apart. Two South poles do the same. This pushing apart is called repulsion.
So we can say it simply:
• Unlike poles attract. North and South pull together.
• Like poles repel. North and North push apart. South and South push apart.
Now repeat the activity, but use a plain iron bar in place of magnet B.
How It Works

An initially unmagnetised iron bar is attracted by either pole. The nearby magnet aligns magnetic regions in the iron, inducing magnetisation. The nearer iron end behaves as the unlike pole. Much of this alignment may disappear when the magnet is removed.
Compare two explanations for attraction: the object could already be a magnet, or it could become magnetised nearby.
Follow the Evidence

A magnet attracts a plain piece of iron. A magnet also attracts the unlike pole of another magnet. So attraction alone cannot tell you whether the thing in your hand is a magnet or just a piece of iron. Both would attract.
For our magnet-or-iron candidates, repulsion rules out initially unmagnetised iron. Attraction does not distinguish the two explanations.
For the magnets and plain iron bars in these experiments, repulsion is the sure test. A bar that repels one pole of a magnet is itself magnetised.

art.svg: <svg class="g6-source-art" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="81.0 1132.0 890.0 173.5248540900393"><svg class="science-illustration ip-art" x="89" y="1140" width="874" height="122.63455497382199" viewBox="19 269 1910 268" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet" data-original-bounds="{"x":80.30576933455416,"y":1016.9073794722935,"w":888.6428568714473,"h":370.1915125239393}"><image href="../../figures/class-6/science/ch04/png/forces.png" x="0" y="0" width="1942" height="809"/></svg><text class="se-caption" x="526" y="1291.634554973822" text-anchor="middle" data-original-bounds="{"x":244.08960510860604,"y":1273.9613680578768,"w":564.5485644587652,"h":23.563486032162473}">Compare facing poles with the observed direction of movement.</text></svg>

blocks.html: Test both ends. If the first end attracts, turn the test bar around and try its other end against the same pole of your known magnet. Repulsion in either trial identifies a magnet. This is why a single observation of attraction is not enough.
A Magnet Near a Compass
A compass needle is a magnet too. So it should follow the same rules.
You will need: a magnetic compass, a bar magnet with poles marked.
Put the compass on a flat table, away from anything made of iron or steel.
Wait for the needle to settle along the north-south line.
Mark a position diagonally beside the north-seeking end, clear of the needle. Slowly approach that position with the North pole, keeping the magnet horizontal.
Watch the needle. Does it turn? Which way?
Move the magnet away. Let the needle settle again.
Reverse the bar magnet and approach the same marked position with its South pole. Keep the distance and height the same.
Watch again.

Sketch the needle direction in each trial. Did reversing the pole change its direction? Did it return when the magnet was removed? Does this match what you found in the investigation with two bar magnets?
How It Works
The needle turns in response to both Earth's field and the nearby magnet's field. The effect acts on the whole needle, producing torque about its pivot.
Reversing the nearby magnet reverses its contribution to the field. A sideways approach makes turning easier to see than an approach exactly along the needle's line.
When a Compass Is Misled
A compass responds to the local magnetic field, including fields from nearby objects. This is also why a compass gives a wrong reading when a magnet, or a large piece of iron, is kept near it.
Can a Magnet Work Through Things?
A magnet pulls a paper clip across a gap of air. But what if something is put in the way?
You will need: a compass, a bar magnet, and flat sheets of wood, cardboard, plastic and glass.
Set up the compass and magnet as in the preceding compass investigation, so the needle is clearly turned aside.
Predict what will happen if you slide a piece of wood into the gap between them. Write your prediction first.
Stand the wood in the gap. Keep both the magnet and compass still.
Watch the needle.
Take the wood away. Try cardboard, then plastic, then glass.
Safety: Use only smooth-edged glass handled by your teacher; do not use broken glass.
Copy these headings into your notebook and record your predictions and observations there.

blocks.caption: Table 4.2 · Does the magnet still work?

blocks.html: Compare the needle directions with and without each thin sheet, at the same separation. Little change is evidence that these sheets do not noticeably screen the field in this setup.
This result is limited to the tested materials and thicknesses. A magnetic field is not a substance flowing through a sheet. Increasing the gap can reduce the effect even without a sheet.
4.5 Things to Try
Now that you know how magnets behave, here are some things to make and try. Work out for yourself why each one works.
A magnetic garland. Hold a bar magnet above a heap of steel U-clips. Touch one clip to the magnet. Now touch a second clip to the first one. Keep going. How long a chain can you hang?

A ball in a maze. Draw a maze on a sheet of card and glue thin strips along the lines to make walls. Put a small steel ball inside. Now hold a magnet under the card and move it. Can you steer the ball out without touching it?
A clip in water. Drop a steel paper clip into a glass of water. Get it out using a magnet, without wetting your fingers or the magnet.
Two racing cars. Secure a bar magnet on each toy car with removable tape or an elastic band. Push them towards each other. Now turn one magnet around and try again. What changes?

Looking After Magnets
A magnet's strength depends on its material and magnetic alignment. Normal use does not use up magnetism like fuel. Heat or strong impacts can disturb that alignment.

Do not drop a magnet, hammer it, or heat it. Strong impacts or enough heat can damage a magnet or reduce its magnetisation; the effect depends on the material. Do not heat or hammer magnets as a classroom test.

Store bar magnets in pairs. Lay the two magnets side by side, with the North pole of one next to the South pole of the other. Place a small piece of wood between them so they do not snap together. Then lay a small piece of soft iron across each end. Keepers provide a path through soft iron linking unlike poles, helping preserve magnetisation in traditional school magnets. Follow the supplied storage advice for other types.

Storage precautions. Keep strong magnets away from compasses, mechanical watches, magnetic-stripe cards and magnetically stored data. Follow the maker’s advice for electronic devices; not every device is affected in the same way.

Summary
• A magnet produces a magnetic field and can attract iron or attract or repel another magnet. Lodestone is naturally magnetised magnetite; artificial magnets are made by people.

• Materials showing strong attraction in our school tests are called magnetic materials. Iron, nickel, cobalt and many kinds of steel are magnetic. Materials not pulled towards a magnet are non-magnetic. Not every metal is magnetic.
• A bar magnet pulls most strongly near its two ends, called the North pole and the South pole.
• Each piece of a broken bar magnet still has both poles. Breaking does not separate a North pole from a South pole.
• Away from nearby magnetic disturbances, a freely turning magnet tends to align with Earth's local magnetic field. This is close to, but not necessarily along, geographic north-south.
• A magnetic compass uses this. Its needle is a magnet that can turn freely, so it settles along the north-south line and shows us direction.
• Unlike poles attract each other. Like poles repel each other.
• A magnet attracts plain iron as well, so attraction does not prove that something is a magnet. For our magnet-or-iron candidates, repulsion identifies an already magnetised bar.
• Thin wood, cardboard, plastic and glass did not noticeably screen the field in our fixed-gap test. This does not establish a rule for all barriers.
Explain these differences to a partner: a magnet and a magnetic material; attraction and repulsion; a prediction and an observation. Give one example from an activity for each pair.

blocks.html: Recognising life through evidence of change
A snail rests on a stone. A seedling stands in damp soil. Both may look still, yet both are alive. Water moves when the ground slopes, but movement alone does not make it living.
Start with a question
A seed and a pebble sit still. What changes could you look for over time to test for life?
10.1  A pebble, a seed and a beetle

Meera places a smooth pebble beside a dry green gram seed. A beetle crosses the windowsill and disappears behind a pot. The beetle makes the easiest decision: it is alive. But the seed and the pebble both sit still. Does that put them in the same group?

A week later, the pebble looks much the same. The seed, kept on damp cloth, has opened. A pale root reaches out and a shoot begins to rise. Something important was happening inside a thing that had looked inactive. This chapter is about noticing such evidence, including changes too slow to see in one glance.
Our question
How can observations help us distinguish living things from non-living things, and follow a living thing from one stage of its life to another?
What you will learn
• Use several characteristics together to recognise life.
• Explain nutrition, growth, respiration, excretion, response and reproduction.
• Investigate what seeds need and how roots and shoots grow.
• Follow the life cycles of a flowering plant, a mosquito and a frog.
• Make predictions, record observations and explain conclusions.

You will need a notebook for sketches and dated records. Write what you expect before an investigation, then record what actually happens. A result that surprises you is useful evidence; it is not a reason to change your record.
10.2  Looking for signs of life

A wind-up toy moves across the floor. A puddle becomes larger in the rain. Neither observation, by itself, establishes that something is living. Movement can be caused by a motor, wind or a push. A puddle grows because more water joins it. Living growth involves processes within an organism: it uses materials and energy to build and maintain its body.

An organism is a living thing. Organisms take in or make food, respire, remove wastes and respond to their surroundings. Over their lives they grow and develop. Living kinds continue through reproduction. These processes form a connected pattern; we should not make a decision from one feature alone.
Improve a first guess
1. Choose six things you can observe: for example, a potted herb, an ant, a spoon, a dry seed, a fallen twig and a battery toy.
2. Record: make four notebook columns: thing; first decision; evidence; revised decision. Leave room for observations over several days.
3. Describe evidence, such as “new leaves appeared”, rather than repeating the decision as “because it is alive”.
4. Conclusion: for an uncertain case, write what you would need to observe next. Do not invent evidence to complete a row.
Living now, once living, never living

A growing tree is living. A fallen, dried piece of its wood is no longer a living organism, though it came from one. A stone was never living. Paper and cotton cloth also come from living sources; their origin does not make the finished objects alive. A cut stem may still contain living tissue and can sometimes grow roots, so examine the particular object rather than its name alone.
A toy that follows light

A light-sensitive toy turns towards a lamp. That is a response, but its body does not grow through life processes or carry out respiration. A designed response does not supply all the other evidence needed to identify an organism.
Pause before you decide

A dormant seed is different. It contains a living young plant whose activity is very slow. Failure to see movement today does not show that the seed is dead. A living seed may begin growing when suitable conditions return.

blocks.html: 10.3  Movement, growth and food

An animal may move its whole body from place to place. This is locomotion. A rooted plant usually stays in one place, yet its parts can move. A flower opens; a climbing shoot winds around a support; a root changes direction as it grows. Movement is wider than walking, swimming or flying. Plants can respond while staying rooted in the same place.

Some plant movements happen quickly enough to watch. The leaves of a touch-me-not plant fold after a gentle touch. Others, such as a shoot leaning towards a window, become clear when drawings or photographs taken on different days are compared. A slow response is still a response.

blocks.html: A plant that catches insects

Sundews, also called Drosera, have leaves with sticky, hair-like structures. A small insect caught on a leaf can trigger movement that helps hold it. Digesting insects supplies extra nutrients, especially in nutrient-poor habitats. The plant still makes sugars using light; catching insects does not replace photosynthesis.
Growth is a change in the living body

Your shoes may become too small as your feet grow. A seedling adds roots, stem and leaves. These are examples of growth. Development includes changes in form and ability: a plant begins to flower, or a tadpole develops legs. Growth and development often occur together, but they do not mean exactly the same thing.
Nutrition
Nutrition is the way organisms obtain and use food and other needed materials. Food provides materials for growth and repair, and supplies energy released during respiration.
• Green plants use light energy to make food from water and carbon dioxide. They also take mineral nutrients from their surroundings.
• Animals obtain food by eating plants, other animals or their products.
• Roots take up water and minerals; they do not normally take ready-made food from soil.
Observe slowly

Choose one existing potted plant. Make a dated sketch on three different days from the same viewpoint. Count leaves and note one change in a growing part. Mark the pot’s position so that moving it does not confuse your comparison. Do not expect every plant to show a visible change within the same number of days.
10.4  Respiration and removing wastes

Place a hand lightly on your chest while resting. Air moves into and out of your body as you breathe. Breathing is the movement of air; respiration is the process in living cells that releases usable energy from food. They are connected, but they are not the same process.

In familiar animals, breathing brings in oxygen needed for respiration and helps remove carbon dioxide. During active movement, muscles need more energy. Breathing usually becomes faster. A parked vehicle does not respire: burning fuel in an engine is not the activity of living cells.
Watch a breathing pattern
1. Prediction: will ordinary walking change your count? Procedure: sit comfortably and count your ordinary breaths for one minute. Count one breath in and out as one cycle.
2. Record: if ordinary walking is comfortable for you, walk gently for a minute, then count again. A classmate may record while you count.
3. Conclusion: rest and repeat the count. Describe the pattern in words; different people need not have the same numbers.
Care while exploring.
Plants respire too

Plants have no lungs, but their living cells need energy. Gases can pass through tiny pores called stomata on leaves and through other plant surfaces. Respiration occurs in living plant parts during both day and night. Photosynthesis requires light; respiration does not stop when photosynthesis starts. A teacher may show stomata on a prepared microscope slide.

blocks.html: Keeping the body’s conditions suitable

Life processes produce wastes. Excretion is the removal of metabolic wastes and excess substances from the body. Animals remove carbon dioxide in breathed-out air; urine carries dissolved wastes, and sweat contains water and salts. Passing undigested food is different from removing wastes made by cells.

Plants also manage wastes. Gases may leave through surfaces, and some unwanted substances are stored in parts that are later shed. Droplets at some leaf tips contain water and dissolved minerals. These droplets can be pushed out by the plant; they are not the same as dew that condenses from the air. A droplet’s appearance alone cannot tell you its source.
Find a stoma. Look for a narrow dark pore between two guard cells. A pore provides a passage for gases; the still photograph does not measure gas movement.
10.5  Responding and continuing life

A change that produces a response is called a stimulus; the plural is stimuli. A sudden sound may make you turn your head. Light, touch, temperature and gravity can act as stimuli. The response is what the organism does after the change. Distinguish the cause from the action that follows it.

blocks.html: Some plants, including amla, change the positions of their leaves between day and night. Such movements are linked to daily light-dark cycles and internal rhythms. A plant response does not require the plant to have eyes, muscles or feelings like ours.
New organisms, not repaired objects

Reproduction produces new organisms of the same kind. A bean plant forms seeds that can give rise to more bean plants. A frog produces offspring that develop into frogs. Reproduction connects one generation with the next, so a kind of organism can continue even though each individual has a limited life.

A young child is living before becoming able to reproduce. Some adults never reproduce. Reproduction is a characteristic of living kinds; it is not a test that every individual must pass at the moment we observe it.
Resting is different from dying

A sleeping animal still respires. A dormant seed has very low activity. Death is the irreversible end of an organism’s life processes. Lack of a visible response during a short observation is not enough evidence to declare something dead. Equally, giving water to a dead organism cannot restart its life.
Use a pattern of evidence

Movement, nutrition, growth, respiration, excretion, response and reproduction describe the living world together. An organism does not display every characteristic visibly at every age or in every condition.
Revisit your evidence

Return to your first notebook list. Revise any decision for which your reason was only “it moves” or “it does not move”. Keep the first entry visible: the change in your explanation shows what the evidence helped you learn.
Compare growth with respiration

blocks.html: The seedling builds its own living body. The pile becomes bigger because material is added from outside. The adult still maintains its body even without a visible increase in size. This is why growth and respiration must be interpreted together rather than treated as interchangeable signs.
10.6  Inside a resting seed

A dry seed may look like a small packet of stored food, but a viable seed also contains an embryo, a young plant. The outer seed coat protects it. In a bean, the large seed leaves, or cotyledons, hold much of the food reserve. These reserves support early growth before the seedling has enough working leaves. The cotyledons are part of the embryo, along with its young root and shoot.

• Observation · look closely at a specimen or image.
• Investigation · compare conditions or follow change.
• Reflection · explain what the evidence supports.
• Recording · make a dated note, sketch or answer.
• Summary · connect the ideas you have learned.
Inside a bean seed
The two thick cotyledons are part of the embryo. They store food that supports early growth. Opening the seed reveals a tiny young shoot and root along the inner edge.

blocks.html: Germination is the start of growth of the embryo into a seedling. The seed takes up water and swells, the coat opens, and a young root usually emerges first. Swelling alone is not reliable evidence: even a dead seed can soak up water.
What starts the change?
A viable seed needs three conditions for germination:
• Water allows growth processes to resume and softens the coat.
• Oxygen supports respiration, releasing energy from stored food.
• A suitable temperature allows these processes to work. Too cold or too hot can delay or prevent germination.

Light requirements vary. Many seeds, including beans and gram, can germinate without light. Some kinds germinate better in light, while others need darkness. Follow guidance for the seed kind being tested.
Germination and later growth
A bean can begin growing in darkness using its reserves. For continued healthy growth, its green seedling needs light to make food, as well as water, air and suitable nutrients.

blocks.html: Four seed groups
Prediction: write which groups you expect to sprout and why, before starting.
1. Label four shallow plastic containers A–D. Place five seeds on tissue in each. Keep A dry; cover B’s seeds with water; moisten C and D without flooding.
2. Put C in a ventilated dark box with light-shielded vents. Keep A, B and D in the same indirect light and all groups at the same room temperature.
3. Maintain each water condition. For 7–10 days, count seeds with an emerging root daily. Inspect C briefly, then close its cover. Record dates, counts and mould separately.
Conclusion: compare A with D for water, C with D for light, and B with D for flooding.
B still contains dissolved oxygen. Flooding limits air access and can encourage decay; it is not a measured “zero oxygen” treatment. Record observations in the table on the next page.
Your observation notebook

Record real results, even if they differ from expectations. A fair investigation includes its uncertainties. The seed packet may be old, the room unusually cold, or a tissue allowed to dry between observations.

Read your record: does “three roots visible” mean that the other two seeds are dead? No. They may germinate later. Keep observing until the planned end of the trial, and report the number that germinated within that time.
Reading what happened

We would usually expect little or no germination in dry group A. Seeds in moist groups C and D should often germinate, showing that these seeds can begin growth without light. Submerged group B may germinate poorly because oxygen becomes harder to obtain. These are predictions, not results to copy into an observation column.
Invented example data

Imagine A has 0 sprouts, B has 1, C has 4 and D has 5 after seven days. C is the important comparison for the light question: four seeds sprouted in darkness. The difference between four and five is too small, in these tiny groups, to establish that light improved germination.
Write: “In this trial, gram seeds germinated in both light and darkness.” Do not write: “Every seed germinates in every dark place.” Temperature, moisture, oxygen and seed condition still matter.
Why moist soil works

Loose soil contains air spaces as well as water. Roots can grow through these spaces. Flooding fills many spaces with water, making oxygen less available. Soil supports a developing plant and supplies minerals, but soil itself is not essential for the first emergence of a root: seeds can germinate on moist tissue. The moist tissue must still allow air to reach the seeds.
Make an observation record
Record daily counts out of five. Zero is a result; a blank means no observation.
Does temperature matter?
Question: does temperature affect germination? Prediction: state which group you expect to sprout first and why.

Procedure: use two groups of ten seeds of one kind on equally moist tissue. With an adult, place one group in a cool location and the other in a warmer, suitable room location. Keep light exposure and air access alike. Record the temperature in each place and count emerging roots daily for a week.
Record: date, temperature, moisture and roots visible out of ten. Conclusion: compare counts and time to the first root in each group.

Repeat with fresh seeds if possible. Compare both how many germinate and how soon they do. Check moisture daily: a warmer group may dry faster. Two temperatures can show a difference, but cannot reveal the best temperature across the whole possible range.
Care while exploring.
Record root emergence separately from leaf opening: they are different events in development.
From the experiment to the grain jar

Keeping stored grains and pulses dry discourages germination and also reduces spoilage. Dry them properly before putting them into a clean, dry storage container. Protect them from moisture and pests. A grain that is not sprouting is not necessarily dead; it may be waiting for conditions that allow growth.

If no seeds sprout in any group, the investigation has not shown that water is unnecessary. Check seed viability and conditions, then repeat. A suitable comparison group that germinates gives meaning to groups that fail.
10.8  Which way will a seedling grow?

A seed can lie in many positions in the ground. Yet its root generally grows downwards and its shoot upwards. If we gently turn a young seedling, the new growing parts can bend. The root does not need to “know” where the bottom of a pot is: gravity is a directional stimulus. Observe the direction of the new tip as the young plant grows.
Figure 10.3 separates the starting position from later growth. Use the same fixed viewpoint in your own observations.
Turn once. Then follow new growth.
A turned seedling grows into a new direction; it does not rotate itself back.

blocks.html: Turn and compare
Question: how does growth respond after turning? Prediction: draw separate arrows for the root and shoot.
1. Germinate gram seeds on moist tissue. Place similar seedlings against the walls of two shallow clear observation containers, supported by damp tissue, above collected water.
2. Keep one upright. Turn the other container a quarter-turn so the root and shoot start sideways. Support it in this new position. Do not pin or bind living tissue.
3. Keep both evenly lit and moist. Mark container corners and draw dated outlines from the same viewpoint for several days.
Record: trace old parts and new tips separately. Conclusion: compare root and shoot directions with the upright control. Record no change if none is visible.
The paper support is illustrative. In class, use damp tissue to support the seedling gently.
When light enters from one side
An upright shoot can bend towards a brighter side as it grows. Keep the pot stable to distinguish a growth response from a change made by moving the apparatus.

blocks.html: Follow the light
Question: will the shoot bend toward one-sided light? Prediction: mark its expected new direction.
1. Place an upright seedling in a ventilated cardboard box with one side opening. An adult should cut the opening. Use indirect daylight; avoid direct sun and overheating.
2. Keep the box closed except for that opening and light-shielded ventilation. Set a similar uncovered seedling nearby. Keep moisture and temperature similar.
3. Mark the pot position. Briefly open the front to sketch both plants daily from the same viewpoint, then close it.
Record: dated shoot outlines and the opening’s direction. Conclusion: compare new growth with the starting outline and the uncovered plant. Restore suitable light after the investigation.

Roots generally grow in the direction of gravity. Shoots generally grow upwards and can bend towards light. These responses occur in growing parts while the plant stays rooted in one place.
Keep the comparison fair

A plant moved nearer the camera looks larger without having grown. Keep the pot, camera and ruler fixed. Record elapsed time and actual ruler readings; also trace the tip’s direction because height alone can miss growth along a curve.

blocks.html: Read the visual evidence
Which image shows the parent, and which shows its offspring?
Check your reasoning. The flowering plant is the parent. The embryos inside the new seeds are offspring. A pod is a fruit of the parent plant, not a new plant.
Keep a plant diary
Question: which changes connect seedling, flowers and new seeds? Prediction: sketch the order you expect before keeping the diary.

Procedure: grow a bean or another suitable quick-growing flowering plant in a pot with drainage. Ask a gardener which kind suits the season. Start a dated notebook record and continue for about three months, or longer if needed. Note the first root, first leaves, new branches, flower buds, open flowers and fruits.

For every new event, record a date, a short description and a labelled sketch. Count days from sowing rather than guessing the plant’s age. Observe which part remains after petals fade and whether a pod develops. If mature seeds form, save some and sow them under suitable conditions.
Conclusion: use dated entries to distinguish development of the parent from production of new seeds.

Many bean plants yellow and dry after completing reproduction, even if water remains available. Trees may flower and fruit repeatedly over many years. Do not turn one plant’s lifespan into a rule for all plants. A plant can also yellow from unsuitable conditions, so yellow leaves alone do not establish that its natural life has ended.
Reading a life diary

A diary records events as they occur, not as a timetable says they should occur. Light, temperature, water, variety and seed condition affect the pace. If no flowers appear by the final observation, write that honestly and continue if possible. A missing event is a result, not an empty space to fill with an imagined date.
A photograph beside each dated sketch can help you compare small changes without disturbing the plant.
Not every new plant begins with a seed

Seeds are one route to a new plant, but they are not the only one. A potato tuber can sprout from a bud, and a suitable stem cutting, such as money plant, can form roots. These are examples of reproduction from plant parts. A florist’s cut flower and a rooted cutting therefore should not be judged only by whether they are detached from a plant.
A seed is missing from the story

Rohan grows a money plant from a stem piece with a node. He says, “It cannot have a life cycle because I never sowed a seed.” His conclusion is mistaken. The cutting can establish a new plant, grow and develop. A seed-to-seed diagram describes the bean example, not every possible route by which all plants reproduce.

To investigate a cutting, sketch the stem before roots appear and again after they develop. Label the node and the new roots. Keep a separate record for the original plant. The new cutting and its parent share a living origin, but their later growth can be followed as separate individuals.
From a living stem
Ask a gardener which stems root readily. Success with one plant does not mean that every detached twig can produce a new plant.
A small field study

During an adult-led garden visit, look for seedlings, mature plants, flowers and fruits. They may belong to different kinds of plants; do not arrange them as one life cycle unless you can identify them. Ask the gardener when one chosen plant is usually sown and when it normally flowers locally.

For a longer project, make a five-plant picture journal with names, dated observations and labelled stages. Distinguish what you observed from what the gardener told you. Leave flowers and seeds where they are unless you have permission to collect them. The journal can show both shared stages and different rates of development.
10.10  A mosquito’s hidden stages
The flying mosquito is only one stage. In the Culex example, a female lays a floating egg raft. Larvae and pupae live in water; a winged adult emerges from the pupa.

blocks.html: Different individuals, not a time-lapse. Egg raft and larvae: Culex; adult: male Culex pipiens. The pupa photograph shows general mosquito form; its species is unverified. It is not evidence that all four specimens belong to one species.
Look for the larva’s long segmented body and the pupa’s rounded front and curved abdomen. The adult photograph cannot show egg laying: the individual pictured is male.

Read the arrows. A larva becomes a pupa; it does not produce one as an offspring. An adult female lays new eggs after mating. The adult reference photograph shows a male, a different individual from these illustrated stages.
One animal, changing form

The larva and pupa are not two different animals. They are successive forms in one mosquito’s development. In many common mosquitoes, both obtain air at the water surface. A larva is usually elongated; the pupa has a larger rounded front and a curled abdomen. A pupa is not a dead larva, even though its feeding and appearance change.
Four stages
Egg → larva → pupa → adult → eggs of the next generation. Major changes in body form during development are called metamorphosis.

Temperature, food, species and other conditions affect development and adult lifespan. There is no single number of days that describes every mosquito. Use dates from a particular observation record when answering a timing question.
How can we find the correct order?

A photograph showing larvae and pupae together tells us that both occur in the container. It does not, by itself, prove which becomes which. To establish a sequence, we need observations of change through time.
Reconstruct a sequence safely
Question: which evidence connects stages? Prediction: write the stage order you expect.

Procedure: use a teacher-provided video or dated picture series that follows individual mosquitoes through development. Record the starting shape, the later shape and the date for each tracked individual. Conclusion: if an elongated larva becomes a pupa, and a pupa later releases an adult, those transitions establish the order.

For a mixed group, repeatedly counting larvae and pupae is less certain: new eggs may hatch and some individuals may die. A continuous recording of a particular individual, or controlled observations supplied by a trained observer, gives stronger evidence.
Care while exploring.
Use the life cycle to prevent breeding

Some mosquitoes transmit infections, including malaria, dengue and chikungunya; different kinds transmit different infections. Knowing where young mosquitoes develop helps us act before new adults emerge. Ask an adult to inspect flowerpot saucers, stored buckets, cooler trays and other artificial containers that collect water.

Once a week, adults should empty and scrub suitable water-holding items, turn unused containers upside down and cover water that must be stored. Record each location, the action taken and a date for checking it again. Natural ponds support many organisms and should not be emptied as a school activity.

An oil film can interfere with air access at the water surface, which explains an example sometimes discussed in textbooks. It is not a classroom treatment: do not pour kerosene or other oils into water. Report persistent breeding sites to responsible adults or local mosquito-control services.
Another insect with four stages

A silk moth also develops through egg, larva, pupa and adult. Its larva, the silkworm, produces a silk thread and wraps itself in a cocoon before becoming a pupa. The cocoon is a protective covering; the pupa is the developing insect inside. The fibres are used to make silk. India’s village-industry organisations, including KVIC, are connected with silk-related livelihoods.

A jelly-like cluster of frog eggs is called spawn. An embryo develops within each viable fertilised egg. In the pond-frog pattern here, a tadpole hatches into water, then develops legs as its body changes.

blocks.html: Compare the legs and tail rather than image size. Hind legs appear before the front legs emerge. The tail is gradually absorbed as the froglet develops; it is not simply cut off.

Identified eggs, embryo and adult are common frogs (Rana temporaria). The tadpole, hind-leg and froglet photographs have no verified species identification. These comparisons illustrate a pond-frog pattern, not every frog species.
Read the photographic sequence
Which arrow introduces a new generation? Which stages still have a tail?
Check your reasoning. The dashed adult-to-eggs arrow marks reproduction. The tadpole, hind-leg stage and froglet have tails, with the tail much reduced in the froglet.

A froglet looks like a small frog but may retain a shrinking tail. Lungs develop and the animal becomes able to spend more time out of water. The tail is gradually absorbed by the body. Stronger legs support swimming and jumping. The adult in this familiar pattern lives in and around water and breathes using lungs and moist skin.

The adult produces the next generation of eggs. A froglet is not yet a reproducing adult. Frogs have varied life histories, so this pond example should not be treated as a description of every frog species.
Compare the photographs by body features, not by image size: each picture has a different scale.
Changing body, changing way of life
The tadpole’s tail and gills support an aquatic life. Developing legs, lungs and a changing body allow the young frog to use a different range of places. Structure and habitat are connected.
Put observations in order

Look for a change that links one stage to the next: an embryo developing in an egg, a tail after hatching, hind legs, front legs, then a shrinking tail. A larger animal is not automatically a later stage if you are comparing different individuals or different species.
A pond from a safe distance
Question: which visible features distinguish the stages you see? Prediction: sketch the features you expect in a tadpole and a froglet before viewing.

Procedure: with an adult, observe from a firm, safe edge, or use a teacher-provided pond video. Sketch only stages you can identify. Note body shape, legs, tail and the place where each animal is seen. Do not label an unknown water animal “tadpole” simply because it wriggles.
Record: use one entry for each sighting. Leave identity uncertain if the features are unclear.
Conclusion: support each stage name with observed features. A mixed group does not show one individual’s development.
Care while exploring.
Read a sample record

In this invented picture record, eggs are seen on day 0, a tadpole on day 6, a froglet on day 60 and a tailless young frog on day 80. The observed interval from tadpole to froglet is 54 days; from froglet to tailless young frog it is 20 days. A young frog is not necessarily a reproducing adult. These are intervals between recorded sightings, not exact stage durations, because a change may have occurred between visits.
To estimate durations more closely, observe more frequently. Do not conclude that all frogs follow this timetable. Species, water temperature and food supply can change the timing.
The cycle in words and pictures

Make a six-frame strip: eggs, embryo in egg, tadpole, tadpole with hind legs, froglet and adult. Draw a final arrow from the adult to new eggs and label it “reproduction”. Write one original sentence under each frame. You can turn the sentences into a short poem, but check that every stage remains scientifically accurate.

Notice that the table groups embryos with eggs and leg-bearing tadpoles with tadpoles. Six drawings and four broad stages need not disagree. They can describe the same continuous development at different levels of detail.
10.12  Patterns across the living world

Plants and animals both grow, develop, use resources and reproduce. A life cycle connects one generation to the next. The stages differ, and some young organisms resemble adults much more closely than others do.

rows.html: Seed → seedling → mature plant → flowers and pods → new seeds
Egg → larva → pupa → adult → new eggs
Aquatic young become a flying adult
Egg → tadpole → froglet → adult → new eggs
Tail and gills give way to an adult body with legs and lungs

blocks.html: Both mosquitoes and frogs have young stages in water, and both undergo marked changes in body form. A mosquito has a pupal stage; a frog does not. A froglet is a young frog with a changing tail, not a pupa. A frog is not simply a large tadpole, just as a winged mosquito is not simply a larger larva.

A chick already resembles a bird: it has a beak, legs and feathers, though its proportions and abilities change as it grows. Birds do not pass through larva and pupa stages. This comparison shows why “all animals change in exactly the same way” is not a useful rule.
Find the common idea
A bean produces seeds; a frog produces eggs. Explain how these very different structures connect generations. Then name one stage that belongs only to the mosquito sequence in the table.
The surroundings matter

Food availability, water, temperature and the condition of a habitat can affect how organisms grow and develop. Compare records within one species before drawing conclusions. A cooler week may slow insect development; a drying pond can threaten aquatic stages. Dates belong to observations made under particular conditions.
What continues?
The same individual does not travel around a life-cycle diagram forever. Individuals eventually die. Reproduction starts new individuals, continuing the living kind.
Observe with care

Caring for living things includes caring for the places that support their stages. Keep rubbish out of ponds, avoid damaging plants during observations and prevent unwanted water collection around buildings. Curiosity and care can belong to the same investigation.
Explain a shared habitat
A learner sees mosquito larvae and tadpoles in the same water and concludes that one will grow into the other. The shared habitat does not support this claim:
• The two belong to different kinds of animals.
• Each follows its own developmental sequence, and each adult produces offspring of its own kind.

In your notebook, draw two separate routes from eggs to adults. Put the mosquito’s pupa on one route and the frog’s leg-bearing tadpole on the other. Add a reproduction arrow to each. This diagram should show what the cycles share without joining stages that do not belong together.
Read a photograph carefully
A photograph preserves one view at one moment. It can show a root, a leaf or an animal’s body form, but cannot by itself show how quickly that organism grew or what happened next.

Choose two photographs from this chapter. For each, write one feature you can actually see and one question the picture cannot answer. For example, an adult frog photograph shows legs, but does not reveal the date on which its tail disappeared. A dated series of observations would provide better evidence for that change.
10.13  Keep the ideas connected
Words to use accurately
Observation: something noticed or measured. Prediction: what you expect before a check. Experiment: a planned investigation of a question. Conclusion: what the evidence supports, with limits stated.

Stimulus: a change that prompts a response. Germination: the beginning of seed growth into a seedling. Habitat: the place and conditions in which an organism lives. Metamorphosis: major changes of body form during development.
What this chapter established
• Recognise life through connected processes. Dormant seeds can be alive.
• Nutrition supplies food and materials; respiration releases energy. Breathing moves air.
• Excretion removes metabolic wastes and excess substances. Organisms also respond to stimuli.
• Growth and development change individuals. Reproduction connects generations. Death ends a life.
• Viable seeds need water, oxygen and a suitable temperature. Light requirements depend on seed kind.
• Roots generally grow down; shoots generally grow up and may bend towards light.
• Plants can reproduce through seeds or from plant parts.
• Mosquitoes develop through egg, larva, pupa and adult. Frogs in the pond example develop through egg, tadpole, froglet and adult.

1 · Using What You Know
Try each question in your notebook before reading its explanation.
Use the chapter’s ideas where evidence is incomplete or a first explanation seems convincing. Decide what each observation can actually establish.
1. Two dry seeds look alike. One is viable and one was killed by strong heating. Both swell on moist tissue. Has this proved that both are alive? What later observation would help?

No. Water can enter material that is no longer living. Swelling shows water uptake, not necessarily the growth of an embryo. If a young root emerges and continues to grow, it provides much stronger evidence of germination. The viable seed may do this; the dead seed cannot resume life processes.

A seed that has not germinated after a short wait is still an uncertain case. It may need more time or different conditions. To interpret its failure, compare it with several known viable seeds of the same kind growing in suitable conditions. Notice how a comparison makes an absence of change more meaningful.
2. A plant is kept in a dark cupboard. After three days, its shoot is longer but its leaves are pale. Does its extra height prove that darkness is best for plant growth?

No. Length is only one measurement. The seedling can use stored food to extend its shoot while searching, through growth responses, for light. Pale leaves and weak growth may show that its development is not healthy. The stored supply is limited. Continued growth of a green plant requires light for making food.

Compare leaf colour, leaf number and sturdiness as well as height. Start with similar seedlings and maintain similar water and temperature. A conclusion about “best growth” needs a clear meaning of growth and more evidence than one long stem.
3. A learner draws the arrow “adult frog → eggs” and labels it “the frog changes shape”. What should the label say, and why?

The label should say “reproduction”. An adult does not change into a cluster of eggs. Eggs begin a new generation, while the parent remains a separate individual. Arrows from egg to tadpole and from tadpole to froglet describe development of an individual; the return arrow has a different role.

This distinction also applies to a plant diagram. A mature bean plant forms seeds inside pods. The next seedling grows from one of those seeds; it is not the old plant starting its life again. A cycle represents continuity across generations, not an individual living forever.
4. A class compares seeds beside a sunny window with seeds in a cupboard. The window group is warmer and its tissue dries faster. Can a difference in germination be assigned to light?

No. Light, temperature and moisture all differ. Any of these could contribute to the outcome. Keep both groups at similar measured temperatures, maintain equal moisture, and arrange light and dark treatments without changing the other conditions. A ventilated cover in the same room can help, provided it does not warm or dry the treatment differently.

Use the same seed kind and several seeds in each group. Check daily. You cannot make a comparison perfect merely by naming it an experiment; the actual conditions must support the question being asked.
5. An adult animal is no longer increasing much in size. It breathes, eats and responds normally. Is “no visible growth” enough to call it non-living?

No. Growth rates change with age, and not every life process is visible at every moment. The animal is maintaining its body and carrying out other life processes. Likewise, an individual that never produces offspring is still living. The living world is recognised by a pattern of processes over a life history.

A useful test of an explanation is to try it on more than one example. “Everything alive must be visibly growing now” fails for this adult and for a dormant seed. Revise the rule so that it explains the evidence without excluding ordinary living organisms.
2 · Behind Each Answer
Choose one answer before reading the reasoning. Each problem has four options.
Problem 1
Which observation gives the strongest evidence that a dry seed has germinated?
1. It darkens when wet.
2. It gains weight on soaking.
3. A root emerges and grows.
4. Its coat peels off.
Explanation

Answer: C. Germination involves renewed growth of the embryo. An emerging root that grows is evidence of that process. The other observations can result from water entering and softening a seed, even if the embryo is no longer alive.
A good answer identifies what is being tested. The question concerns germination, not simply whether water entered the seed.
Now distinguish the start of growth from the needs of an established seedling.
Problem 2
Two groups of the same viable seeds are kept equally moist and warm. One is in light and one in darkness. Both germinate. What is supported?
1. These seeds can sprout in darkness.
2. Darkness makes germination faster.
3. Light is needed for the first root.
4. Later growth needs no light.
Explanation

Answer: A. The result concerns the tested seed kind and the beginning of growth. It does not describe every plant or later development. B claims a speed difference that was not reported. C contradicts the dark group’s germination. D confuses germination with the light needs of continued growth.
The strongest conclusion is often the one whose scope matches the experiment. A broader statement is not automatically a better explanation.
Problem 3
A seedling with an upward-pointing root is kept moist in even light. Several days later, what is most likely?
1. The root grows straight up.
2. New root growth bends down.
3. The whole root rotates at once.
4. The root grows toward the shoot.
Explanation

Answer: B. A young root generally responds to gravity by growing downward. Turning the seedling changes its starting position, not gravity’s direction. A overlooks the growth response, C mistakes new growth for rotation of the whole root, and D assigns the root the shoot’s usual direction.
The existing root may retain a bend. We predict the direction of new growth, not that all older tissue will suddenly rotate.
A gradual change needs observations across time. The same is true when we investigate the order of animal stages.
Problem 4
Which sequence links the observed stages of one mosquito correctly?
1. Egg → pupa → larva → adult
2. Larva → egg → pupa → adult
3. Egg → larva → pupa → adult
4. Egg → larva → adult → pupa
Explanation

Answer: C. An egg hatches into a larva; the larva develops into a pupa; an adult emerges from the pupa. A reverses larva and pupa. B begins with a developing larva producing an egg, which is not the sequence. D places the pupa after the adult.
A photograph of several stages together is useful for identifying shapes. Evidence of one stage becoming another is needed to confirm their order.

A single picture can identify a form, but it cannot usually establish how that form developed. A dated series following the same organism connects earlier and later observations. A drawing of the final adult alone cannot tell us which immature stage came just before it.
Problem 5
A school wants to reduce mosquito breeding in unused water containers. Which action best follows from the life cycle?
1. Keep the water until the adults emerge.
2. Ask adults to empty and scrub suitable containers regularly.
3. Collect larvae and raise them in class.
4. Pour kerosene into nearby ponds.
Explanation

Answer: B. Removing breeding water and cleaning suitable containers interrupts development and removes eggs that may remain on surfaces. A allows development to continue. C creates an avoidable breeding activity. D introduces a harmful household chemical into a habitat; it is not a student action.
The question concerns unused artificial containers. It does not justify draining natural ponds. A good application preserves the conditions in the question.
Read the reasoning as well as the letter

The five answers depended on five distinctions: soaking versus germination; starting growth versus continuing growth; starting position versus new growth; coexisting stages versus an observed sequence; and a biological explanation versus a suitable action. Each distinction comes from the lesson rather than from a new topic.

Before moving on, choose one wrong option from each problem and explain it aloud. State what the option confuses, then give the correct relationship. “It is wrong” is a verdict; “it reverses the larva and pupa stages” is an explanation.
Keep the evidence in view
Ask what was observed, what was changed, and how far the conclusion reaches. A record can support an explanation without settling every possible question about the organism.

Write a two-sentence explanation for an adult: name the young stages that use water, then explain why cleaning a container should happen before adults emerge. Keep the biological reason and the proposed action clearly connected.

4 · Answers & Takeaways
Check the reason for each choice, then revisit any idea you confused.
Set A
1. A. Respiration releases usable energy in cells. Breathing moves air, nutrition supplies materials, and excretion removes wastes.
2. B. The touch is the stimulus. Folding is the response. The changed position or shape of a leaf describes a response, not its trigger.
3. C. The coat protects the interior. Cotyledons hold most stored food; the embryo’s young root and shoot grow into the seedling. The coat does not become these organs.
4. D. The adult emerges from a pupa. Egg and larva occur earlier. A winged mosquito is already in the adult stage.
5. A. The muscular tail propels a young tadpole. Gills support breathing; egg jelly surrounds the embryo. Undeveloped legs cannot do the swimming work shown.
6. B. Carbon dioxide is a waste made during respiration. Taking in food or oxygen is not waste removal; passing undigested food differs from excretion.
Set B
1. C. Motion can be mechanical and a seed can be dormant. None of the definite classifications follows from motion alone.
2. D. The trial shows that soil was not required for initial sprouting. It does not remove the need for oxygen or establish claims about later nutrition.
3. A. Stored reserves supply the developing seedling. Water is needed but is not its food reserve. Soil food is not a requirement for sprouting, and growth needs energy.
4. B. Legs develop while the tail is gradually absorbed. The tail does not become legs or drop off before the legs develop.
5. C. C changes water while controlling seed kind and temperature. The other comparisons change extra conditions or compare different materials.
6. D. Living origin and present life are different questions. B and C incorrectly use movement as a decisive test.
Set C
1. A. A pod can contain seeds of a new generation. The parent remains distinct from its offspring. New embryos develop inside seeds, not as roots growing directly inside a pod.
2. B. The young aquatic stages include larvae and pupae. An adult is one of four stages, so the reason is false.
3. C. A pupa is a living developmental stage. Not feeding at a particular stage does not establish death.
4. D. The conclusion must remain within the temperatures and seed kind tested. A generalises beyond the trial; B confuses delayed germination with death. C ignores the water provided to both groups.
5. A. A tracked transition links stages directly. Counts alone can change because of hatching, death or movement. The other records do not show the required transition.
6. B. Both undergo major development, but their stages differ. Both begin as eggs; the mosquito adult flies and the pond-frog adult uses water and land.
Three things to carry forward
Look for a connected pattern of life processes. Match a conclusion to the comparison actually made. Read life cycles as development of individuals linked by reproduction between generations.
